I

MARTIN DAVID PERRY
Grand Master – 2015-2016

Brother Martin “David” Perry was raised a Master Mason at Silverado
Lodge No. 782 in Napa on March 23, 1988. He served his lodge as Junior
Warden in 1993. Following consolidation with Napa Valley Lodge No.
93, David served as Master of Napa Valley Lodge in 1996. He continued
to assist his lodge after his term as Master and was recognized with the
Hiram Award in 1999.
Brother Perry has served the Grand Lodge of California for more
than 15 years. In 2000, he was appointed a District Inspector and acted
in that capacity for nine years. In 2008, he was appointed the Assistant
Grand Lecturer for Division I and served four terms until he was
elected Junior Grand Warden in 2012. David has served on the Grand
Lodge Ritual Committee, the Inspectors Training Sub-committee, and
the Executive Committee. He has also been a member of the board of
directors for the Masonic Homes of California, Acacia Creek, California
Masonic Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple, and Nob
Hill Masonic Center.
David is a member of Napa Chapter No. 30, Royal Arch Masons, and
has received the Royal and Select Master Degrees He is a member of
the Scottish Rite Bodies in the Valley of Oakland, the Aahmes Shriners,
Saint Francis Conclave of the Red Cross of Constantine, and Silver
Spray Chapter No. 59, Order of the Eastern Star.
David has been very active with the Masonic youth orders. He has
servied as a member of the advisory council for Napa Chapter, Order
of DeMolay, and has received the honorary DeMolay degree for King
Solomon’s Chapter. He is a past member and chairman of the advisory
board of Napa Assembly No. 7, International Order of Rainbow
for Girls, and has served multiple terms as Rainbow Dad. DeMolay
International honored David with the Honorary Legion of Honor.

MARTIN DAVID PERRY

Grand Master
October 11, 2015 – October 29, 2016

David has been active in the Hopewell Baptist Church and Napa
Valley Baptist Church, where he has served as a Sunday school teacher,
director, and trustee.

David lives in American Canyon with his wife, Jeanette. They have
two adult children, Nicholas, who is a Mason and a Senior DeMolay, and
Courtney, who is an active Rainbow Girl serving as a grand officer from
2014-2016.

3

One Hundred Sixty-Seventh
Annual Communication
Friday Afternoon, October 28, 2016
The 167th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand
Master M. David Perry on Friday, October 28, 2016.
Worshipful Brother Charles E. Cunningham, Jr., Past Master of
Napa Valley Lodge No. 93, raised the opening session of Grand Lodge.
The gavel used to raise Grand Lodge was commissioned by the Grand
Master during the opening of the XIV World Conference of Regular
Masonic Grand Lodges last November.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand
Marshal to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of
California at the altar. The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past
Grand Master, following which the Grand Master, accompanied by the
Deputy Grand Master, personally greeted each one. The Grand Master
asked the brethren to join him in saluting our Past Grand Masters by the
battery of three times three. The Past Grand Masters were then escorted
to seats reserved for them in the auditorium. The Grand Master then
directed the Grand Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master
the usual letter of greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge
Officers, Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain
if a constitutional number were present to convene the Grand Lodge of
California. The following were present as indicated by their response to
the calling of the roll:

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Memorial Service

A special request for our fellow brothers and sisters who serve in
uniform: Continue to bless all who stand in defense of our communities,
our nation, our constitution, and the precious ideals of democracy. Give
them your strength, grant them forgiveness as warriors, and let them
know your unending love.

The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend John M. Hinck,
Grand Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed
brethren. His remarks were as follows:
JOHN M. HINCK
GRAND CHAPLAIN
No great undertaking in life is risk free or free from loss. And all
service eventually comes to an end. Many in our Masonic family no
longer walk with us in our journey of Brotherly Love, Relief, and Truth.
Their time has ended on this earth, but their names and memories live
on, giving us strength. We ask your special blessing on all those who
have passed to the heavenly gates. It is fitting, therefore, that we pause
with a few reflections of time honored words.
Our fallen brothers may say:
Death is nothing at all. I have only slipped away into the next room.
I am I, and you are you. Whatever we were to each other, that we still
are. Call me by my old familiar name, speak to me in the easy way which
you always used. Put no difference in your tone, wear no forced air of
solemnity or sorrow. Laugh as we always laughed at the little jokes we
enjoyed together.
Play, smile, think of me, pray for me. Above all, continue to be
Masonic with me.
In reply, one might beseech our Lord,
Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death,
I will fear no evil,
for you are with me;
your rod and your staff,
they comfort me.
Yet, together, we do pray,
God our Father,
Your power brings us to birth,
Your providence guides our lives,
And by Your command we return to dust.
Give us strength to do Your duty,
And unending wisdom to do Your will.

As we remember our fellow brothers during this memorial pause,
elevate our thoughts, strengthen our virtues, and purify our minds, thus
preparing us for own admission into the society of the blessed in the
realms of life and light eternal.
Thank you for this glorious day. May we continue to live by thy will
as we sound the resounding hymn in glory and praise to your name:
Alleluia, Alleluia, Alleluia! In your name we humbly pray, amen.

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

17

Most Worshipful John L. Cooper, III, Past Grand Master, then
delivered a eulogy for the late Past Grand Master Charles H. Alexander.
Charles Herbert Alexander was born on July 27, 1927, and died on
November 8, 2015. He served the Masonic Grand Lodge of California
as Grand Master from October 11, 1995 to October 16, 1996. A native
Californian, Most Worshipful Bro. “Charlie,” as we all called him, was
born in Chico of a five-generation family of farmers. At the end of his
earthly journey he died in Chico, a beloved and respected citizen of
that community.
Charlie was preceded in death by his beloved wife, Greta, who died
the April before.
Charlie was a schoolteacher – a teacher of United States history
and of civics – and for a few years served Chico High School as a Vice
Principal. But his first love was teaching, and he taught in the classroom
for most of his 35 years as a credentialed teacher. Generation after
generation of high school students knew and loved Charlie, and he lived
to see several of his former students become Masons in Chico Lodge
No. 111 – which is now Chico – Leland Stanford Lodge No. 111.
Most Worshipful Brother Charlie was often heard to say that
there were four cornerstones in his life: his family, his profession,
his church, and Freemasonry. Charlie and Greta had two sons and
three grandchildren. He was an active member of St. John’s Episcopal
Church in Chico, serving as a licensed lay reader and Lay Eucharistic
Minister. Both the York Rite and the Scottish Rite benefitted from
Charlie’s leadership. He presided over all the bodies of the York Rite,
and was honored as a Knight of the York Grand Cross of Honor. He was
a Thirty-Third Scottish Rite Mason, and a Past Venerable Master of the
Sacramento Lodge of Perfection. In addition, he served as Sovereign of
St. Francis Conclave of the Red Cross of Constantine.

Our Father, by whose servants
Our house was built of old,
Whose hand hath crowned her works,
With blessings manifold,
For thine unfailing mercies,
Far strewn along the way,
For all who passed before us,
We praise thy name today.
The changeful years unresting,
Their silent course have sped,
New comrades ever bringing,
In comrades steps to tread,
And some are long forgotten,
Long spent their hopes and fears,
Safe rest they in thy keeping,
Who changest not with years.
They reap not where they labored,
We reap what they have sown,
Our harvest may be garnered,
By ages yet unknown,
The days of old have dowered us,
With gifts beyond all praise,
Oh, Father make us faithful,
To serve the coming days.

20

21

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Report on the Recognition of the
Grand Lodge of Georgia and the
Grand Lodge of Tennessee

I suspended recognition of these grand lodges for two reasons. First,
their actions are a violation of the General Regulations of Freemasonry.
Second, their actions threaten the reputation and good standing of our
grand lodge.

Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
On March 7, 2016, I notified the Masters and Wardens of our
Constituent Lodges that I suspended recognition of the Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Georgia and the Grand
Lodge of Tennessee, Free and Accepted Masons. These grand lodges
had recently adopted new rules or exercised existing rules that punish
Masons because of their sexual orientation.
On September 8, 2015, the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
Georgia issued an edict that amended the Georgia Masonic Code to
include homosexual activity as an act of unmasonic conduct subject to
punishment by their grand lodge. At their annual communication on
October 27, 2015, the members of the Grand Lodge of Georgia adopted
the Grand Master’s edict and the Georgia Masonic Code was amended.
A similar rule exists in the Masonic Code of the Grand Lodge of
Tennessee, wherein promoting or engaging in homosexual activity is
a Masonic offense. Through a Masonic trial initiated in the summer of
2015, two Masons under the Grand Lodge of Tennessee were suspended
for an indefinite time period for posting on Facebook photographs of
their marriage to each other. At their annual communication on March
24, 2016, the members of the Grand Lodge of Tennessee defeated
resolutions that would have repealed this rule and restored these
brothers to membership.
These events made national news. Local and national television
stations, radio stations, newspapers, and websites carried the
story about Masons banning and punishing men because of their
sexual orientation.
In late February, I met in person and separately with the Grand
Masters of Masons in Georgia and Tennessee. In these meetings, I
learned firsthand what was occurring in their jurisdictions and I worked
to understand their motivations, which I found to be of a religious and
political nature. In these meetings, I explained how the actions of these
grand lodges were affecting the reputation Masonry in general and the
Grand Lodge of California in particular.

The actions of these grand lodges violate the General Regulations
of Freemasonry because they impose a particular religious, if not also
political, view on the fraternity. This particular view is not one on which
all men in this country agree. No regular grand lodge may do this.
Anderson’s Constitutions of 1723 and the requirements for recognition
make this clear.
Anderson’s Constitutions of 1723 oblige a Mason to obey the moral
law. The moral law prescribes the standards to which the actions of
people should conform in their dealings with the Supreme Being, each
other, and themselves. However, the moral law includes only those
sectarian rules and principles on which all men agree. Consistent with
this point, Anderson’s Constitutions of 1723 oblige a Mason to that
religion in which all men agree, leaving their particular opinions to
themselves. Thus, no discussion is allowed in a regular lodge of Masons
on any sectarian rule on which Masons have differing yet genuinely
held beliefs, nor may a regular lodge or grand lodge take a position
on any such rule. The Standards of Recognition of the Commission
on Information for Recognition of The Conference of Grand Masters
of Masons in North America addresses this point also. Among other
requirements, these standards condition recognition on a grand lodge’s
prohibition of the discussion of religion and politics. By this prohibition,
we live up to the centuries-old aim of our fraternity – to unite men of
every country, sect, and opinion and cause true friendship among those
who otherwise would have remained at a perpetual distance.
All grand lodges are sovereign and may make their own rules. We
are not questioning the sovereignty of these grand lodges, but under
our California Masonic Code a grand lodge must adhere to the General
Regulations for us to recognize them.
The actions of one grand lodge can affect other grand lodges, as
has happened in these instances. The reputation and good standing of
the Grand Lodge of California has been harmed by the actions of these
grand lodges.
Within weeks of the publicity of these events, the Grand Lodge of
California was the focus of protests and our community partners began
to question their association with Freemasonry. Protests took place

22

23

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

in front of our Grand Lodge building during the World Conference, at
public facilities where we were conducting ceremonies, and at schools
and universities where we have established important programs. A
website emerged called “Mason bigotry,” which claimed that all Masons
were bigots and encouraged the California public to call our community
partners and our business partners - including our tenants in the
Memorial Temple – and tell us to end the discrimination.

I also heard from many Masons in California - from Entered
Apprentices to Past Grand Masters - who asked me what we were going
to do about this situation and called upon me to take decisive action.

A Boys and Girls Club where we were scheduled to perform a
cornerstone ceremony was besieged with phone calls and emails
demanding that the cornerstone ceremony be cancelled. We worked
closely with the CEO and the board of directors who had a number
of questions about Freemasonry, our grand lodge, and our relationship
to the grand lodges in Georgia and Tennessee. Fortunately, that
cornerstone went on as scheduled, though protestors disrupted it.
For seven years now, we have enjoyed a partnership at UCLA
where classes are being taught on the subject of Freemasonry and
where we sponsor an annual international conference on the subject of
Freemasonry. Protestors and members of the public called and wrote to
university leaders and urged them to cancel our March conference. They
urged the university to terminate Dr. Margaret Jacob for her support
and personal work on our partnership. Fortunately, the university
stood with us.
Not all of our community partners responded as favorably. Two
cornerstone ceremonies were cancelled at schools named for Masons
or Masonic families because the school district could not reconcile the
value of the ceremony with the risks of the public protests.
We were about to embark upon our annual public schools month
in April with events at various schools around the state. We were
about to launch the 2016 Masons4Mitts campaign, which fosters our
partnerships with the San Francisco Giants, the Los Angeles Dodgers,
and the San Diego Padres.
The Grand Lodge of California has worked very hard to maintain
strong community partnerships. These help us remain relevant and
respected in our state. Protecting these relationships was critical to me
as Grand Master.
Let me be very clear. I would stand up to any amount of public
pressure to defend the principles of Freemasonry. But our public
partners were not attacking the principles of Freemasonry. They were
asking us to live up to them.

I have been asked why I took action on this issue when some of
these same grand lodges have not had mutual recognition with the
Prince Hall Grand Lodge in their jurisdiction. Recognition is a matter
of mutual agreement between two regular grand lodges. It is not fair
to assume and very difficult to prove that a grand lodge which does
not enjoy mutual recognition with a Prince Hall Grand Lodge is
discriminating on the basis of race. We have sought recognition from
Prince Hall grand lodges that do not want mutual recognition with us.
But, let me be clear again. The Grand Lodge of Georgia and
Tennessee adopted or exercised rules that punish a brother because of
his sexual orientation. If a grand lodge were to punish a brother because
of his race or the color of his skin, it would be a violation of the General
Regulations of Freemasonry and I would respond in the same way.
Believing that something is wrong, but being reluctant to do
anything about it, subjects Freemasonry to a certain understandable
scrutiny by Masons and the public. I’ve often said and I truly believe,
that if you are clear about your values, difficult decisions are easier to
make. In suspending recognition of these grand lodges, we made it clear
that their actions were wrong and that the Grand Lodge of California
does not condone these actions.
I believe our grand lodge should continue the suspension of
recognition of these grand lodges until they chose to operate according
to the principles of our Institution.
Should either of these grand lodges change their rules at their next
Annual Communication or at any future time and end their punishment
of Masons because of their sexual orientation, I believe our Grand
Master should restore recognition at that time and not wait until our
next Annual Communication.
Therefore, I move that the Grand Lodge of California continue the
suspension of recognition with the Grand Lodge Free and Accepted
Masons of Georgia and the Grand Lodge of Tennessee Free and
Accepted Masons according to the terms and conditions set forth in my
March 7 communication and that the suspension remain in effect until
recognition is restored by Grand Lodge or by the Grand Master.
The motion was seconded and adopted unanimously.

Presentation of the Joe Jackson Award
Joe Jackson, a Mason for 60 years and Hiram Award recipient,
served Joseph L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837 and Heartland Lodge No.
576 for 17 years as secretary, assistant secretary, treasurer, and chaplain.
Joe exemplified Masonic relief and brotherly love. He reached out
to members and widows regularly, assisted with numerous applications
to MOS and the Masonic Homes, and frequently called Masonic
Assistance to check the status of his members’ applications. He
connected members and their families not only to Masonic services but
also to community resources and programs for veterans.
Through his tireless efforts, Joe was a catalyst for launching
the Lodge Outreach strategic initiative in Division IX. Joe passed
away in 2012, leaving a legacy that set the foundation for extending
Masonic Relief.
The Grand Master went on to explain that the Joe Jackson Lodge
Outreach Award is given to a lodge that has demonstrated excellence
in outreach to their members and widows. The Joe Jackson Lodge
Outreach Award was presented to San Dimas Lodge No. 428 in San
Dimas, for their extraordinary outreach efforts this year.
Masonic Youth Leadership Scholarship Awards
This year, the California Masonic Foundation created the Masonic
Youth Leadership Scholarship for the youth leaders of the four Masonic
Youth Orders in California. The Masonic Youth Leadership Scholarship
focuses on a particular segment of the talented, dedicated and deserving
members of these youth orders – their state and regional leaders. These
leaders include the Rainbow Grand Assembly Officers, Job’s Daughters
Grand Bethel Officers, and the DeMolay jurisdiction, division, and
league officers. There are approximately 100 such youth leaders in any
given year. All Awardees present joined the Grand Master on the stage
for recognition.

Mason of the Year and the Builder Award
This year, we were proud to honor Brother Thomas W. Moberly
with two meaningful distinctions: The Mason of the Year Award and the
Builder’s Award.
The Mason of the Year award is a very special award bestowed
by our Grand Master to recognize one brother’s extraordinary
accomplishments. Instituted in 1978, this award has only been given
out 10 times in its history. Although there are many distinguished
brethren in our jurisdiction, this award honors Brother Moberly for his
heartfelt service to our craft and devotion to his fellow man. Brother
Moberly has been an exceptional example of what it means to be a
Mason, a leader, a mentor, and a man.
Brother Moberly has been a Mason for more than 54 years and is a
member of Martinez Lodge No. 41. In addition to his Golden Veteran’s
Award, in 2008 he was awarded with the Grand Master’s Youth Service
Award for his extraordinary efforts on behalf of Masonic youth.
It is also because of these efforts that we honored him with a special
new distinction envisioned by Grand Master Perry: The Builder’s Award.
Like the Mason of the Year Award, the Builder’s Award is awarded to a
Mason who has made an extraordinary difference – who has risen to
the occasion to build a deep impact on the future of our great fraternity.
Nowhere is this initiative demonstrated more clearly than through
Brother Moberly’s devotion to building the next generation of our
Masonic family. Brother Moberly has been a part of DeMolay for more
than 60 years – even more time than the organization’s founder, Frank
S. Land. He received his DeMolay Degree in June of 1955 in Ferndale,
Michigan, and as a young man, was honored within DeMolay with the
Chevalier Active Legion of Honor Cross of Honor – the highest honor
conferred by DeMolay International. Since then he has gone on to
mentor and serve thousands of young men, many of whom have been
inspired to become Masons because of his shining example.

THOMAS W. MOBERLY
Masons of the Year

Brother Moberly served as a past state outstanding DeMolay in his
home state; after moving to California, brought his leadership skills to
fruition by serving as executive director for many years. In 2014, he was
inducted into the DeMolay Hall of Fame for his many accomplishments.
True to his humble nature, he responded to his nomination with
the humble words: “I only hope that my involvement has helped the
DeMolays that I have met and influenced to reach their full potential.”

American Flag Tribute
“I often wonder if Betsy Ross knew of the profound impact she
would leave on so many people, when she sat down to sew the first
American flag. Did she understand that what she was about to create
would soon become a symbol of freedom and bravery? Did she know
the flag would travel and serve as a beacon of hope on every battlefield
that our country would fight? I wonder if she realized it would leave
our Earth, and arrive at the moon? Did she realize it would stand for
the freedom and independence that only America could have? Was she
aware the cloth she was stitching would become a source of comfort for
those that gave it all for the freedoms we have today? Did she realize
when she stitched those 13 stars, that eventually it would grow to 50?
Did she dream it would wave just as proudly today, as it did when
she held it in her hand? Could she have imagined that the flag would
become a symbol of patriotism, courage, and opportunity for so many
Americans? I wonder if she was aware that the flag she sewed would
end up being America’s most recognized symbol and it would be flown
proudly from atop government buildings, churches, colleges, and many

40

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

homes across America. Did she understand that her flag would become
one of the most powerful symbols of Americanism? What about the
songs that would be written about it and school children who would
pledge to it every morning? As long as the American flag stands high
and waves, it will serve as a symbol of freedom, independence, unity,
and equality. I can only hope that Betsy Ross was proud of the flag she
created, and knows what an important piece of history she made. May
we ever remember that the cloth she held in her hand, woven together
stitch by stich, is even more empowering today, than it was when she
created it.”

to raise someone up by making a lasting impression on his or her life.
To show you what I mean, I’d like to share a story with you about
something that happened years ago. A young girl was invited to a Job’s
Daughter event and soon after she joined the organization and became
a part of a family that was bigger than she could ever realize. Many
wonderful years passed and when she had two daughters of her own,
they joined Job’s Daughters and now two generations were involved
in the Masonic family. But this story isn’t just about these two young
girls. No, this story is about their father. Their father was not a Mason,
nor was he involved in the Masonic family until his daughters joined
Job’s Daughters. He loved his daughters and loved watching them
grow, mature, and learn in this beautiful organization. He watched as
they learned many lessons about steadfastness, respect for our elders,
kindness to others, and respect for our country and flag. And I’m sure
that somewhere along the way he thought to himself, If my teenage
daughters can learn all of these life skills from this Masonic family, then
why can’t I?

MISS HEIDI JOHNSON, GRAND WORTHY ADVISOR
INTERNATIONAL ORDER OF RAINBOW
“Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers and members of Grand
Lodge, distinguished and honored guests, and friends of California
Rainbow: Good afternoon! I am extremely honored to have been asked
to speak to you on behalf of the International Order of the Rainbow for
Girls in California.
This afternoon I want to share with you something rather, different.
I grew up in a very small town in Northern California. Each fall as
the leaves started to turn in color and harvest was in full swing, geese
would start migrating. I can remember hearing the honking of the flock
and would look to the sky to see the V-formation as it passed overhead.
But what I didn’t realize then was that the beauty of the migration lies
not in where the geese were headed but rather how they got there. The
signature V-formation that geese travel in is not just for looks, but is
actually designed to cut wind resistance, allowing the geese to travel
up to 70 percent farther with the same amount of energy as one goose
could accomplish alone. If a goose falls out of the formation, it suddenly
feels the drag and resistance that comes with flying alone and quickly
returns back into the formation to take advantage of the lift that the
flock offers. As the group pushes forward, the lead goose, taking on the
majority of the wind resistance, becomes tired causing another goose
to step up and take the lead. In order to successfully transition leaders,
the flock will communicate and encourage each other to keep going
with their honking. The foundation of success for this migration though,
rests in that shift of the lead goose position. This action reminds us of
the importance of teamwork, leadership, communication, and loyalty.
When we share a common goal, our success is dependent on the
support we provide each other and the commitment we have to the
guiding principles of our Masonic Family. These principles are best
shown when our leaders set the example through their attendance at

46

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

events, their participation in the community, and their investment of
time and resources in the future of our orders. While we are challenged
to take chances and work towards the goals of our own organizations,
we must not forget that united we make a profound difference. We must
rise and build.

MR. JESUS MARTINEZ, MASTER COUNCILOR
SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA JURISDICTION,
DeMOLAY INTERNATIONAL

Through our Masonic family we learn the tools needed in order to
be great leaders. Our ritual reminds us that though elevated for a time
being, we must eventually return to the ranks. Just like the geese as they
rotate their lead position during the migration, we too must realize that
change brings new ideas and through our loyalty to the foundations and
members of our organizations, we will continue to move forward.
We learn to stand by our sisters and brothers and lift them up in
times of need. A little encouragement can go a long way, and can help
an individual achieve more than they thought they were capable of. At
Masonic functions, we are constantly in a positive environment, there
is always a sister, brother, mom, or dad, to encourage us in whatever
task we are facing. It is that loyalty to the members of our Masonic
organizations that makes us a family - a family that is devoted to serve
those around them.
So I encourage all of you to reflect on the significance of the geese
migration and its deeper meaning. I urge you to remember your roots;
remember what began your story in the Masonic Family. I hope you
communicate not only within your organizations, but also within the
entire Masonic Family. We can only help each other when we know
that a need is present. Most importantly, I hope all of you protect what
is most valuable. Protect our Masonic Family. Protect our virtues and
lessons. Protect our heritage by supporting one another through acts of
love as they come to you in opportunities of service. Thank you.”

“Good morning Grand Master Perry, Distinguished East, Masons of
California, and guests. It is my privilege to speak to all of you today
on behalf of the members of Southern California DeMolay. Traveling
with me here today are our Southern California Jurisdiction Officers:
Deputy Master Councilor Mitchell Bowman, Congress Secretary Avery
Brinkley, Sweetheart Jazlyn Magana, and Princess Hailee Powell.
Our theme this year is ‘Mt. Olympus: Champions of DeMolay!’ and
it has two meanings. First, it means that we rise to the challenge to be
the best DeMolay that we can be. And its second meaning is that we
build our jurisdiction to new heights of leadership and brotherhood.
Thankfully we have our Masonic Family to help and guide us on
this odyssey.
Our philanthropic program for the year is focused on community
service and donating man-hours to help our community and show the
public what DeMolay stands for and what DeMolays can accomplish
when we work together. Chapters have already taken the initiative and
are working on finding project opportunities. Some are volunteering
at the Midnight Mission. Some are planning neighborhood or park
cleanup days. And some are sponsoring families in need during the
holidays that are not able to afford gifts for their children or even have
a decent family meal. I know members that are in similar conditions as
those we are trying to help. They come from broken homes or troubled
families. Some don’t fit in everywhere or are tormented and bullied
at school. Thankfully they have found a safe haven in the Order of
DeMolay. When they attend a meeting or event, they know they are in a
safe place, surrounded by friends.
This reminds me of the story behind the founding of DeMolay.
97 years ago a Mason by the name of Frank Sherman Land saw
troubled teens in need of a safe place and mentors to guide them. ‘Dad
Land’ created something that still to this day inspires young men to
challenge themselves to change the world for the better. Over this timespan many of these young men have gone on to be successful leaders
because of what they learned in their DeMolay Chapter, and what they
learned from the Masonic family.

Whether it is in Santa Barbara, Long Beach, Chula Vista, or Indio
– wherever we meet – we are bound together by a fraternal bond
that cannot be replaced. It is the chapters that are the foundation of
DeMolay, as well as the foundation that they will build on for the rest
of their lives. I personally have seen myself and many of my brothers
raise and build themselves into successful leaders that will some day
change the world.

Every time we step into that lodge room we know that we can make
a difference, and you can too. Whether it be in DeMolay, in your lodge,

is one of the most powerful boosts you can give a person for success.
I want to thank all of you on behalf of my brothers for believing in

that together we will rise and build a better world. A DeMolay is only

Masons of California, DeMolays have the finest cornerstone on which
to build their future.

One of our future leaders was a young Squire of New Valley Manor
located in San Fernando. For those of you that don’t know what Squires
are, it is an organization for young boys between the ages of 9 and 12
that has principles very similar to DeMolay. This young boy by the
name of Ethan Struebbe became Master Squire of his manor, which
is the equivalent of Master Councilor of a chapter. His philanthropic
project for his term was for the Alzheimer’s Association and he wanted
to raise$1,000. He started a Go Fund Me account and everywhere I saw
him he was carrying a small red bucket so that people could donate any
spare change they had. At the end of his term, he had collected$1,350
in donations.
Another young DeMolay named Christopher Cruz from Conejo
Valley Chapter also exemplifies the virtues of leadership and
brotherhood at such a young age. He was initiated at our Grand Master’s
Membership Class, where he received both degrees, when he was just
12 years old. Throughout the 2015-2016 DeMolay year he decided to
challenge himself and learn some of the hardest ritual that DeMolay
has to offer. Then at Conclave 2016 this past September, he was selected
to play the roll of Jacques DeMolay for our Grand Masters Class. In just
one year Chris had gone from being initiated at Conclave, to performing
Jacques DeMolay, which is one of the most intricate parts of our ritual,
in front of the International Master Councilor and Grand Master
of Masons in California. This young man at 13 years old has become
one of the best ritualists in our jurisdiction and he has just started his
DeMolay career.
These are just two recent examples of the DeMolay success story.
This is what we in DeMolay can accomplish and plan to accomplish this
year and for many years to come.
I invite you to join us on our Odyssey - to support a chapter project
or event, to work with a chapter, or be a mentor to a young man.

Thank you!”

Michael received the Distinguished Service Award and Degree of

Brother Lenaburg has been an invaluable asset to Job’s Daughters.

future generations.

Grand Master’s Message
Most Worshipful Past Grand Masters, fellow Grand Lodge Officers,
Inspectors, Masters, Wardens, distinguished guests, and all brethren here
assembled, I welcome you to the 167th Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge of California.
RISE AND BUILD
Our theme this for this Masonic year has been “Rise and Build.” As
a strong and united Fraternity, we have taken every opportunity to rise
together to build Freemasonry in California. We rose our sights to the
future and launched our 2020 Fraternity Plan. We rose to the occasion
for brothers in need and to overcome obstacles together. We built new
programs and services. We built new lodges and supported those that
were struggling. We built and strengthened relationships with each
other, creating lifetime friendships and memories that will sustain us
throughout the years to come. When I look back, I am in awe of what we
have accomplished together.
Last year, I knelt before you and took a solemn obligation to serve
as your Grand Master. In that moment, I asked myself if I was indeed
capable of rising to the occasion, of serving as a tool to build this great
craft. How would I inspire you? What tools would I offer to ease your
way? What answers and solutions would I provide?
I found these answers as I needed them by calling upon the wisdom
and help of my brothers. As time passed, I realized that what I truly
needed to build was a better me. Freemasonry teaches us all again
and again how to become better men - not better than other men,
but better than ourselves. By improving David Perry, I would be more
valuable to the brothers around me and, together, we would build a
stronger Fraternity.
Freemasonry has always been about building. In ancient times we
were craftsmen, working with quarried stone to build great cathedrals.
Today we are still builders, but craft with stones far more fragile,
precious, and valuable. We are building up ourselves and other men. We
are living stones, and together we form a temple. Our great masterpieces
are our lives.

All year, in Grand Lodge and in blue lodges statewide, we have
worked side by side with our brothers towards the same goal: Rising to
build our Craft. And, together we have done just that.

continue to be shared around the world.

2020 PLAN
Our first order of business was to launch the 2020 Fraternity Plan.
More than 7,000 California Masons helped to build the framework
for this plan, which serves as our blueprint for the next five years.
Our brothers identified four plan priorities – a Rewarding Member
Experience, Meaningful and Memorable Degrees, Strong Lodges and
Halls, and Our Impact on Society. We worked on this plan at all of the
leadership retreats this year. Now lodge leaders are developing plans for
their lodge around these priorities. Together we will turn this blueprint
into reality and build a stronger fraternity ready to meet the demands
and expectations of a new generation of men seeking further light
in Masonry.
As Grand Master, I have worked to achieve certain priorities in this
plan and I want to share some of the highlights with you now.
XIV WORLD CONFERENCE
In November, regular Freemasonry in California welcomed the
world to San Francisco for the 14th World Conference of Regular
Masonic Grand Lodges. I say, “regular Freemasonry” because all three
regular grand lodges practicing in California – our Grand Lodge, the
Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, and the Grand
Lodge of Iran in Exile – came together to show everyone that California
Masonry is united. Though we practice in our own grand lodges with
diverse rites and practices, we share a common vision of Freemasonry.
Our chain of union is strong and vibrant.
The World Conference brought more than 1,000 people, representing
106 grand lodges to our Memorial Temple. It was the largest conference
in the program’s history. During the opening ceremony, our Masonic
youth presented 55 national flags, acknowledging the countries of every
guest. We presented 11 books of Holy Writings.
In our opening ceremony, the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge
of Iran in Exile and the Grand Master of the Most Worshipful Prince
Hall Grand Lodge of California joined me in lighting the conference

RELATIONSHIPS WITH OTHER JURISDICTIONS
Hosting the World Conference was a key component of our work
this year to strengthen California’s relationships with other grand
lodges so that we may learn from them as we work on our 2020 Plan.
Building on our teamwork from the World Conference, we continued to
build fellowship with the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of
California and the Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile, learning more about
each other and becoming closer brothers and friends. I thank the Prince
Hall Grand Lodge for joining us in Masons4Mitts. I was so proud to
stand beside their officers on the ball field. I am also grateful to the
Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile for the courtesies they have extended to
me over the years. I will value our time together and the friendships
we’ve made for the rest of my life.
The grand lodges on our southern border were an important focus
this year, as well. Since the late 1970s, we have held “The Conference
of the Three Californias” with the Grand Lodge of Baja California
and the Grand Lodge of Baja California Sur. This year, we hosted the
conference in San Diego and our Mexican brothers helped provide a
very meaningful experience. These brothers take the lessons of the
craft very seriously, and their spirit of fraternity is strong.
As you may know, our Grand Lodge chartered three lodges in the
Philippines in the early 1900s, which later formed the Grand Lodge of
the Philippines. In Masonic vernacular, we are their “Mother Grand
Lodge.” Many of our brothers today are from the Philippines or have
family there. Together with our history, we celebrate a very special bond
between our jurisdictions.

In May, the Grand Secretary and I travelled to Manila and to
Tagaytay for the 100th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
the Philippines. I was the first sitting Grand Master of California to make
such a visit. Their hospitality was tremendous. From when brothers met
us at the Manila airport at 4 a.m. until we departed, they treated us
like royalty, fulfilling our every need and desire. Their hospitality should
serve as an example of how to treat visitors to our lodges. Every guest
should feel important, needed and accepted. I thank our brothers from
the Philippines for extending this friendship and brotherly love.

Our Philippine brothers could not join us today, but I had the
opportunity to see their Grand Master earlier this month. During this
meeting, I presented him with a special gift. When we visited their grand
lodge museum in the Philippines, we saw that the original charters
granted by our Grand Lodge were on display. Like many historic
documents, they had been tattered and torn over time. When we met
on October 2, I presented replicas of these three original charters as a
gift to their museum. Now, everyone who goes there can read the full
charter and understand our strong and enduring bonds.
As you know, our fraternal ties to the Grand Lodge of Georgia and
the Grand Lodge of Tennessee were challenged this year. Suspending
recognition was a serious decision and we have continued to monitor
the situation closely. Tomorrow afternoon, I will offer a full report on
the suspension along with my recommendation for moving forward.

Two of our new lodges opened in downtown San Francisco where
men are clamoring to become Masons, and a new lodge rose in downtown
Los Angeles, where a once-declining population is flourishing. In
Fresno, brothers started a new lodge to bring Masonry to Central Valley
universities. In Benicia, which has less than 50,000 residents, there
was sufficient interest to institute two new lodges. Roseville, a town of
125,000, now also has two active lodges. These lodges will bring vitality
to the Masons establishing them, the Masonic family surrounding them,
and the communities into which they will grow. Over the next five years,
we will continue this focus on building new lodges with the right people,
in the right location, and for the right reasons.
Though I continued the suspension of two lodges at the beginning
of this year, I am pleased to report that both of these lodges – North
Hollywood Lodge No. 542 and Menlo Park Lodge No. 651 – had their
charters restored. I want to thank the brothers of both lodges, and
their Inspectors and Assistant Grand Lecturers, for working together
to renew and rebuild Freemasonry in their community. Moreno Valley
Lodge No. 804 surrendered its charter this month. Currently, there are
no lodges under suspension.
AGL INSPECTORS ROLES AND TEAMWORK

NEW AND RENEWED LODGES
At the same time that we were strengthening ties with brethren
far away, we have been building new lodges throughout California, in
cities that are underserved by Freemasonry. Although the District of
Columbia has roughly the same population as San Francisco, that city
has 44 lodges – many more than the nine we had here in San Francisco
at the beginning of this year. Half of California cities and towns have no
Masonic lodge at all.
We created 10 new lodges in our state this year – the most since
1958. Seven have received a dispensation and more are underway. Most
encouraging, each new lodge is led by brothers with a vision for our
fraternity and all are located in areas that will benefit from Masonic
representation and engagement. Our new lodges often have fewer
members than other California lodges, but when we look around the

Another important structural focus this year was updating the roles
of our Assistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors who support our local
lodges. We realigned the jurisdiction into nine divisions and increased
the average district size from three to four. We are improving training
programs to prepare Inspectors for their important duties as managers
in our Fraternity.
At this time, I would like to recognize three of our Assistant Grand
Lecturers who are retiring this year. Worshipful Brothers Jeff Wilkins,
Lynn Wallingford, and Doug Eichen: We are grateful for your dedicated
service to our Fraternity.
The Executive Committee has carefully considered new brothers
to appoint to these open positions. We will also be filling the Assistant
Grand Lecturer position of Worshipful Brother John Trauner, our Junior
Grand Warden Recommendee, should he be elected. Thank you to
everyone who has participated in this process.

BUILDING OUR YOUTH ORDERS
As we strengthen our brotherhood, we must also lift up the Masonic
youth who follow in our footsteps. They are the future of our country
and our fraternity.
If you know me at all, you know that the Masonic youth orders
captured my heart and devotion years ago. My son, Nick, is a Senior
DeMolay and my daughter, Courtney, is a Rainbow Girl. They are
talented, intelligent, and caring young adults, and the principles they
learned and experiences they enjoyed as Masonic youth have guided
them in becoming the wonderful people they are today.
I have proudly volunteered as an adult advisor for both
organizations. It has been one of the most rewarding experiences of
my life, and I encourage you to do the same. Our youth depend upon
us to serve as adult volunteers and to provide safe, affordable meeting
places. They need our financial support for programs that will help
them develop into successful adults. And, we must set an example by
modeling the principles of Masonry.
This year, we rose together to help strengthen our youth orders,
and there are three achievements in particular that I hope will endure.
The first of these is advancing our efforts to promote our youth, talking
and writing about them whenever possible. On a state level, they were
represented in the California Freemason magazine, member emails, and
lodge officer newsletters. Many lodges also worked to actively promote
Masonic youth through their websites and Trestleboards. I thank those
who did so and encourage all lodges to follow their example. If there is
not a youth order in your town, promote those closest to you. One day,
this could lead to a bethel, assembly, or chapter in your town.
The second initiative I would like to praise is Leadership Experience
2016 – Lx2016 for short. Through this new program, we held two
weekend conferences for youth leaders, which focused on teaching
principled leadership techniques. The outstanding training and positive
youth responses inspired our Executive Committee to plan to continue
this program for at least two more years. Many people contributed
to the success of Lx2016, but in particular I would like to recognize
Worshipful Brother James Banta, our former Assistant Grand Secretary,
and Very Reverend Brother John Hinck, our Grand Chaplain, for their
crucial roles. Brothers, thank you for your dedication in leading this
great program for our youth!

The third initiative I am pleased to share is our new Masonic Youth
Leadership Scholarship, a$3,000 scholarship awarded by the California
Masonic Foundation to youth leaders who are serving or have served
in regional or statewide leadership positions. Like our Grand Lodge,
the Masonic youth who fill leadership roles contribute an extraordinary
amount of time, often traveling throughout the state to attend functions
in support of their peers. Many of these young people are college-age
and must sacrifice their studies to fulfill leadership duties. This new
scholarship recognizes their efforts and facilitates their ability to attain
the education they deserve. I will be honored to award 22 recipients
with this scholarship during tomorrow evening’s awards ceremony.
To facilitate these important programs, I reorganized the Youth
Orders Committee. I want to thank the members of that Committee,
and their Chairman, Most Worshipful Brother Larry Adamson, for
dedicating themselves to these young people who need our support
now more than ever.
REDEDICATION TO GIVING
There are others in our Masonic family who depend upon us, too.
Our ritual calls us to practice Freemasonry’s tenets outside the lodge
as well as in it, to be ambassadors of our Fraternity by exemplifying
good deeds, to “be the one to whom the burdened heart may pour out
its sorrows.” As such, Relief is central to our character and culture.
We are committed to performing acts of charity and kindness, both
as individuals and as a Fraternity. Together, we provide critical relief
for Masonic family members in need and vital support to California
communities, particularly our public schools.
Thanks to the generosity of the brothers who came before us,
we have built a substantial endowment to provide relief. But the
distribution from the endowment only covers about 65 percent of the
annual cost to provide relief. Remaining funds must come from other
sources, including our own charitable gifts. This year, we rededicated
ourselves to giving, asking each brother to give to our Annual Fund
according to his own ability. I couldn’t be happier with the results or
more proud of the thousands who joined us. More Masons gave this
year than any since 2010. We have more Anniversary-Level gifts and
Grand Master Circle members than ever before.

MAKING A MASON AT SIGHT
When I speak of rising to the occasion for brothers in need, I must
share with you an experience I had this year with one of our brothers
in his final days in this world. Thanks to Worshipful Guadalupe Thomas
and the other brothers of Naval Lodge No. 87, I had the rare honor of
making a Mason at sight.
Mr. Brian Shields applied to receive the degrees of Masonry, but
due to a grave illness, he was told he only had a few days to live. His
dying wish was to be made a Mason. On the day we raised him, several
brothers formed a Chain of Union around Brian and, with Brian’s son
present, I proceeded to make him a Master Mason. Brian was so happy
to become a Mason that for a brief moment, his pain subsided. The
joy we shared together was unforgettable. I couldn’t imagine a more
rewarding gift, not only for Brian but for all of us. I will never forget his
smile and the sparkle in his eyes. Oh, how he had longed for that day,
and how he loved his lodge and his brothers! And, while his journey on

Worshipful Brother Guadalupe, I thank you for being a living
example of Freemasonry in action by helping our brother achieve his
final dream – to join our great fraternity. You are what we all hope to
become: a true example worthy of imitation.
RAISING MY SON A MASTER MASON
Finally, I cannot look back at this year without mentioning the
Masonic event that was not only the most meaningful of my year, but
perhaps of my life – raising my son, Nick, to the degree of Master Mason.
I believe every father longs for the day when his son becomes a
Mason. It was a dream I hoped would come true for Nick and me. As
I mentioned earlier, Nick learned of Masonry at an early age through
DeMolay. He grew up in our lodge and saw me serve as Master. I was
sure he would ask to join Masonry, first when he turned 18, then when
he was 21. But it wasn’t until my installation as Grand Master last year
that he gave me the happy surprise of his application for degrees. I can’t
begin to tell you the feelings that came over me that day and again as I
witnessed each of his degrees.
I obligated Nick, and after his Entered Apprentice degree, he told
me: “When I heard your voice, I knew everything was going to be OK.”
The evening of Nick’s Master Mason degree was even more special,
as it took place in my home lodge, with your Grand Lodge Officers by
my side. Along with Nick, we raised the son of the Master of my lodge.
Both young men were from the same DeMolay chapter. It was a moving
experience and – oh, what a joy. That night has been one of my fondest
memories and I was honored to share it with my Grand Family.
My hope is for all fathers to share in the joy of passing Freemasonry
on to their sons. Just imagine how strong our lodges would be if we
included all of our sons, sons-in-law, nephews, and grandsons! I am
so grateful to my brothers and friends, including Mike Stern, Russ
Charvonia, Allan Casalou, Jordan Yelinek, and Larry Adamson, who
kept patiently showing Nick the value in our Craft, and how welcomed
he would be to stand beside us.

Thank you, Nick, for becoming a Freemason. I hope that you will
continue to be inspired by your membership, that you will make true
friendships that last a lifetime, and that you will become the best man
that you can be. I am very proud of you.

Grand Master’s Calendar

Thank you, my brothers, for allowing me the opportunity to serve
as your Grand Master. It has been a true honor and privilege to share
this year with all of you. I will always treasure your faith in me and your
friendships. You have helped me to become a better man. Like a rock in
the quarry, you molded me and helped me to polish my own living stone.
This stone is not perfect. I never will be. But I will keep working on
shaping my stone, on becoming better for myself and for our fraternity.
I know you will do the same, because that is what Freemasons do.
Keep building, my brothers. Keep building and never quit!

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

89

Report of the Deputy Grand Master
2016-2017 Grand Lodge Budget
John R. Heisner, Deputy Grand Master
Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
The Masters and Wardens of our Constituent Lodges along with
the other members of Grand Lodge approved the per capita proposal I
made as Senior Grand Warden at the last Annual Communication. I am
grateful for the support and I’m pleased to present this budget for your
consideration at the upcoming Annual Communication.
We have made refinements to the budget based on the actual
membership numbers that we have now finalized. We also now have
a more clear idea of the actual costs of some of the time sensitive
initiatives, like lodge insurance and health care. In the spring, I
presented this budget to the Masters and Wardens who attended the
leadership retreats. I received good input from them at the retreats and
some of them have reached out to me since then with questions and
ideas. I appreciate their assistance.
Now that we have the benefit of the latest information, the expenses
in the final budget are actually less than in the budget I presented at
the retreats. In addition to the support from our Masters and Wardens,
I have received tremendous assistance in preparing this budget from
the Grand Lodge Finance Committee, the Executive Committee, the
Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary, our Chief Financial Officer, and
the entire Financial Services team. We have a strong team of Masons
and finance professionals who worked together to create a solid budget
for our grand lodge.
At the 2015 Annual Communication, an additional$1.00 per capita
assessment was approved to support the George Washington Masonic
National Memorial, which was not included in the budget presented
in 2015. This has now been added to the budget, both in revenue and
expense. We have also added a line item for the background check fees
and expenses, which earlier had been a net expense in another category.
Other than these changes, the overall income and expense for the next
fiscal year is very close to what I presented last year.
The total membership ended up about 360 members lower than
we anticipated. The assumption we used when I requested a per capita
rate of $42.50 was 47,757 billable members. The actual number came

90

in at 47,396. In the final result, there were fewer initiations in the year
than we expected. This also caused us to reduce the anticipated number
of applications in 2017. Fortunately, the dividend from the Nob Hill
Masonic Center will be higher than expected, so the there was not an
impact on the balanced budget.
Expenses exclusive of depreciation for the next fiscal year are
estimated to be$3,078,443. These expenses are divided between
fraternal, appropriations, programs, and general and administrative
expenses. The expenses are essentially at the same level as presented
at the 2015 Annual Communication.
The projected net revenue after expenses is approximately$9,700.
As is the practice of our grand lodge, if elected Grand Master, I will
monitor the budget very closely each month and seek the assistance of
the Executive Committee, Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary, and the
Finance Committee to see that we operate according to this budget.
This proposed budget allows us to continue the programs and
services that are important to our members and our fraternity. This
budget will allow us to focus on our 2020 Plan: engaging our members,
strengthening our lodges and halls, building new lodges, and having an
impact on society. As we celebrate the 300th Anniversary of Freemasonry,
we can be proud of our grand lodge and each of our lodges for the good
work we do together!

Expense Analysis

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue sources have been per
capita and degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates income from
the investment return. To better manage the income from the Endowment, a four and a half-percent spending
policy has been instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year average valuation to protect the fund principle. The
Grand Lodge may from time to time have other income, such as interest from bank accounts and other
financial instruments. In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included in its mission the funding of
Masonic education and leadership training programs and now provides a grant for such purposes. In 2005,
the delegates of the 156th Annual Communication adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to Grand Lodge by
all applicants for the degrees of Masonry and out-of-state affiliations. The Grand Lodge manages different
service bureaus throughout the state and receives reimbursement for expenses incurred with the performance
of those services. The Grand Lodge also manages the investments of its related entities and receives
reimbursement equal to the cost of providing those services. The Grand Lodge is the sole shareholder of the
Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc., and may receive dividends on the profits of this Corporation.

Let me start by thanking the Masons of Division VIII – from Riverside
and San Bernardino Counties – who spent so much time working with
me to put together the video we just enjoyed. Wasn’t that a fantastic
journey through 300 years of Freemasonry?A lot of teamwork went into
that production: brothers working together to accomplish a common
goal. This should sound familiar. Masons everywhere have exemplified
teamwork throughout the past 300 years. And, as we enter a new
Masonic year in California and embrace our five-year 2020 Fraternity
Plan, teamwork will be more important than ever before.
What an honor it is to be with you all in this magnificent auditorium.
This “jewel of Nob Hill” is a tangible example of the spirit of charity that
California Freemasonry is known for worldwide. It’s also a great example
of Masons working together to achieve something great. In the early
1950s, our brothers formed a team, set goals, and worked hand-in-hand
to build this beautiful edifice. Its construction was made possible by
gifts from Masons of the generation who fought in World War II – those
who Tom Brokaw has coined “the greatest generation.” These brothers
lived throughout California, from Oregon to the Mexican border. Some
of them never had an opportunity to visit this building themselves, yet
thanks to their amazing generosity, we are meeting here today and may
gaze in wonder at the unique depiction of our Masonic history within
the beautiful endomosaic mural in the lobby. Our “jewel of Nob Hill”
opened in September 1958. Nearly 60 years later, it continues to serve
as a landmark of California Masonry’s core values. It reminds each of us
of our obligation to relieve brothers in distress, provide for each other’s
welfare, and rejoice in our shared prosperity. Standing here, in the heart
of California Freemasonry, let us renew the commitment each one of us
once made at the altar of Freemasonry – to never to forget any one of
our brothers, now or ever.
Indeed, our love for and reverence of history is another defining
characteristic of our great brotherhood. This oldest of all worldwide
fraternities, whose eldest grand lodge, the United Grand Lodge of
England, was established on June 24, 1717, will celebrate its 300th
anniversary this coming year. As many of you know, Masons around

100

101

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

the world gather to mark June 24 each year. We call this celebration
St. John’s Day, in honor of St. John the Baptist, who, together with St.
John the Evangelist, is regarded by Masons as a patron saint. Although
the concept of a “patron saint” may sound religious, allow me to dispel
you of this notion: Masonry is not a religion, never has been, and never
will be. We revere these men as role models to whose character we can
aspire as we work to become better men. Our fraternity builds good
men from bricks made of virtue, fastened with the mortar of morality.

childhood literacy, one public school at a time. We will build new
Masonic lodges and rejuvenate others. We will enhance the fraternal
experience of every Mason through a renewed effort to explore and
deeply understand the profound lessons revealed through our ritual.
We will bring men who might otherwise have remained at a perpetual
distance together to work in harmony and build character in others, and
we will relieve the distressed among us.

To mark this milestone fraternal anniversary, Margo and I invite you
to join us in celebrating St. John’s Day next year in London. It will be a
fitting finale to our Masonic journey to Ireland, Scotland, and England,
which will take place from June 12 to June 26. We hope you will join us
in exploring the landmarks and traditions that are our history. Together,
we will build lifetime memories, gaining a deeper understanding of how
Freemasonry’s past can inform our fraternity today and inspire how we
might plan for the future. It will be a once-in-lifetime adventure and it
would be our great honor to experience it beside you!
Many know Freemasonry as “the greatest fraternity in the world.”
Time and again our brotherhood has benefitted the world through
its vast transformative powers. Working together, our brothers are
capable of transforming hatred into love; loathing into compassion;
and intolerance into a peaceful acceptance of those who have different
appearances, religious practices, or lifestyle choices than our own.
This commitment to embracing diversity in good men is a power that
continues to have the capacity to change our world.
Through Masonic values and practicing teamwork, our brothers
have always led the quest for human freedom: the freedom to say
anything that doesn’t harm others; the freedom to embrace any
religion; freedom from fear, including fears of poverty, indignity, hate,
and intolerance; and the freedom to seek and pursue the knowledge
required to retain these treasured liberties. The freedoms born in the
laboratories of Masonic lodges are Freemasonry’s greatest gift. And,
they are the foundation upon which our Grand Lodge will build upon
in the coming year and beyond, as we look forward to the next 300 years
of our brotherhood.
Our 2020 Fraternity Plan that will guide the next five years begins
today. It is a plan that we worked together to envision, and through
which we must continue to work together to make possible. Together,
we will rescue children from a lifetime of uncertainty by improving

It is our obligation to relief that inspired those who preceded us
to build our incomparable Masonic Homes at Union City, in the San
Francisco Bay Area, and in Southern California at Covina. Today, we
must stand on our forefathers’ shoulders and continue their example of
what Masons do best: ensuring both our young and aging Masonic family
members will live well; that they will be taken care of. Today, we care for
the most vulnerable among us by supporting residents at our Masonic
Homes, providing outreach to brothers in need throughout California,
and helping struggling and abused youth through the Masonic Center
for Youth and Families.
For the next 12 months it will be my pleasure to lead you, to learn
from you, and to do my best to inspire us all to be better men than we
are today. Then, we shall say to each other with great conviction: Our
best days lie in the bright pathways ahead, lit by the gentle glow of the
lanterns of our forefathers.

Report of the Senior Grand Warden
Per Capita Recommendation for 2017-2018
Bruce R. Galloway, Senior Grand Warden
Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
The California Masonic Code requires the Senior Grand Warden to
prepare and present to the Grand Lodge a proposal for the per capita
assessment that will be collected in 2018 to fund the operations of
Grand Lodge fiscal year for the period of November 1, 2017 through
October 31, 2018.
I have worked with our leadership team and staff to develop
projections of the income and the necessary expenses for the 2017/2018
fiscal year. Earlier this year, I shared these plans with the Masters and
Wardens who attended our spring leadership retreats. I very much
appreciate the comments and input I received during and following
the retreats.
In preparing a draft budget for the 2017/2018 fiscal year, I have
considered the factors that will increase per capita, as well as those that
will reduce any necessary increase.
The major factors that will increase the per capita are:
• Membership decline. We project a total loss of 1,896 billable
members. This represents a loss in revenue of $82,476 or $1.81
in Per Capita.
• Fraternal, Appropriations and Program Expense: These three
areas of expense, combined increased by $13,629 or $0.30 in
Per Capita.
• Personnel costs. Wages are held to a 3% increase. Total Personnel
costs will increase by 3.5%. Personnel cost increases of $49,051
represent $1.08 in Per Capita.
• Non-Labor Expense Inflation. Items subject to inflation are
expected to increase by 2% to 3% representing$5,971 or$0.13 in
Per Capita.
Per Capita would need to increase by $3.32 to cover the effect of all
of these factors discussed here.

106

GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED
MASONS OF CALIFORNIA

The factors that will partially help offset the per capita increase are
the following:
• Revenue Improvements. Revenue Improvements in investment
related income and other income totaling $14,380 offset some
of the Per Capita increase by $0.32.

PROPOSED PER CAPITA

$46.50

Fiscal Year 2017/2018 (FY18)
Bruce R. Galloway, Senior Grand Warden

REVENUE

• Cost savings. We identified a number of expenses that can be
held at or near last year’s levels, which takes pressure off of
Per Capita. You will notice that the expenses in many categories
are nearly the same as the budget presented by the Deputy
Grand Master.
These factors allow us to present a balanced budget, with a
Per Capita assessment of $46.50, which includes $1 for the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial. Considering financial effect
of the loss of members, the Per Capita increase represents a modest
1.1% over 2016/2017.
With your support for this proposal, our fraternity will be able to
continue all of the programs and services that are important to our
members, lodges, and grand lodge. Together, we can fulfill our goals in
the 2020 Plan and build a stronger and brighter future for our Craft.

REPORT OF THE Grand Treasurer
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren All:
In this, my first report to you as your Grand Treasurer I am pleased
to report to you that the overall financial health of our Grand Lodge and
related entities remains strong. This is due to the efforts and expertise
of so many brothers volunteering their time as Board Members and
Committee Members, as well as the expertise of our entire Grand Lodge
Financial Services team led by: Tom Boyer, CFO; Maribel Pasamic,
Controller; Khalil Sweidy, Director of Financial Planning; and of course,
Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, our Grand Secretary.
The Audit Committee has been working with our outside auditors,
Moss Adams, to ensure that our financial statement audits for all
of our Grand Lodge entities continue to go smoothly. As of our last
fiscal year ending October 31, 2015, each of our entities continued to
receive a clean audit opinion. Our Audit Committee has continued to
be impressed with the knowledge and professionalism of Moss Adams
and agreed to continue to retain their services for both the audit and
tax work. In addition to these responsibilities, the Audit Committee has
continued their ongoing work in reviewing and updating our Lodge and
Hall Association Audit Guides.
The Finance Committee continues to work with our Deputy Grand
Master and Senior Grand Warden each year to provide wise and
timely counsel in the preparation of their annual budgets and per
capita determinations.
The Insurance Committee has been diligent in their detailed review
and analysis of our ever growing insurance needs for not only our
Grand Lodge entities but also for our lodges and hall associations. They
continue to review ongoing claims to ensure an optimal result for the
benefit of the craft and to look for ways to do all of this in the most cost
efficient manner.
The Investment Committee remains ever vigilant in monitoring
the economic factors which impact our portfolio. They also continue
to evaluate our asset allocations and investment policies resulting in
their continued recommendation that 4.5 percent of our investment
portfolio be distributed to fund operating budgets, which will also work
to preserve and grow our overall portfolio for future use.

In the last several years, we have passed legislation allowing for our
lodges to transfer their Life Membership Funds and also their General
Investments to the Grand Lodge as an option in their investment
strategies. As of July 31, 2016, we have 32 lodges participating in the
Life Membership Master Fund with a value of $933,484 and we have
one lodge participating in the Lodge Investments Master Fund with a
value of $10,886.
We continue to have lodges and hall associations experiencing
challenges with budgets, investments, payroll matters, tax filings, and
general accounting matters. I encourage not only those facing these
challenges, but all lodges and hall associations to reach out to your
District Inspectors for guidance. These men are knowledgeable in the
many resources available to you through our Grand Lodge such as
Intacct training, tax preparation services, payroll services, investment
guidance, audit guidance, real estate matters, and many others. In
utilizing these services and the expertise of our Grand Lodge staff you
will able to focus more of your attention on practicing Masonry within
your lodge.
I would also like to encourage you to begin your budget discussions
as early as possible including advice from those within your lodge
such as your prospective Wardens, Treasurer, Secretary, Trustees, Hall
Association Directors, and those with experience in such matters.
Discuss your budgets openly and frequently so that the finances of your
lodge do not become one of the mysteries of Freemasonry.
Lastly, I would like to thank all of you for the opportunity to serve
you as Grand Treasurer. I have thoroughly enjoyed this year working
on your behalf with so many caring and dedicated individuals. I would
also like to offer my special thanks to Very Worshipful Allan Casalou for
his business acumen and tireless efforts which have brought increased
efficiency and professionalism into the operations of our Grand Lodge
and related entities for the benefit of all California Masons.

Report of the Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge:
I am pleased to present to you this, my ninth report as your
Grand Secretary.
This was a year of significant progress in our Fraternity. With
the launch of the 2020 Plan, a number of new programs and services
are being implemented at every level of the organization. There is a
vitality among our brethren as we chart the course of Freemasonry in
the 21st Century.
Though I’ve heard it said for years, I have noticed this year more
than ever, a true focus on quality in the organization. The conversation
about the number of members has been replaced with a focus on the
fundamentals of Freemasonry. As we look to 2020, the Fraternity will be
a little smaller than it is today. It will also be younger and more diverse.
The men coming to Freemasonry today are not seeking to belong to
largest organization in the world. They are seeking the substance that
Freemasonry offers. They are looking to make true friends, learn and
improve themselves, and have an impact on society.
MEMBERSHIP INFORMATION
As of June 30, 2016, we had 50,694 active members and 24,080
Masonic widows in our database. This membership figure includes
3,172 Entered Apprentice Masons, 964 Fellow Craft Masons, and
46,558 Master Masons. Nearly 2,400 are newly initiated, affiliated, or
restored brothers. This is balanced by 4,042 losses, bringing our overall
membership number slightly lower than last year. The average age of
our members is 59 and the average age of a new member is 38. A more
detailed report of membership activity, together with a number of lodge
bylaw amendments, life memberships, and veterans’ awards, is included
in my written report, which will be distributed in the Proceedings.
The 2020 Plan calls for strong lodges and halls. We are working
together to be sure our lodges have sound administration, healthy
financial plans and systems, and a sound financial and operating plan
for our halls and buildings. We aim to build strength through new
lodges and strong lodge leadership in all lodges. More than ever before,

118

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

our lodges and our Grand Lodge are working together to build our
capacity in these areas, so that lodge leaders and members are not as
burdened by the administration of their lodge and can focus on a quality
member experience.

PROGRAMS AND SERVICES
This new century has brought with it many opportunities to advance
the ways in which we lead and manage our lodges. Technology-based
tools in particular offer excellent benefits, but tend to require some level
of skill, training, and time for research and implementation. As such, it
can be challenging for lodges to take advantage of new developments in
a timely and consistent manner.
We have been actively working to identify the most valuable services
and make them more accessible to lodges and halls. The services, now
offered on a statewide level, have never been greater.
Member Services
Acting as a central source of information, our Member Services team
provides core support to lodge and members. This year, they conducted
more than 1,500 background checks for applicants and processed
nearly 2,000 awards and recognitions to members and widows. They
processed bylaw amendments and dispensations, helped build new
lodges, and guided consolidating lodges through necessary processes.
On top of this, they responded to thousands of telephone and emailbased requests for information and services.
In order to evaluate effectiveness in serving our members, we
implemented a new Salesforce solution to track all information and
service requests that were received and resolved. We received nearly
8,000 requests this year. Since implementing Salesforce, we know that
71 percent were completed within the same business day, with a median
turnaround time of three hours; 98 percent were completed within the
same week they were received.
Our membership data system, iMember, is the most advanced of any
grand lodge in the world. That’s a bold statement, and it is true. iMember
is customized especially to meet our particular membership needs. It
contains deep Masonic business logic and is capable of interfacing with
financial and fundraising systems, postal systems, and others. Every

One important function of iMember is feeding information to our
Member Center, where every California Mason can access his member
record and those of his lodge. A few years ago, we introduced The Vault,
a digital document storage solution that allows lodges to electronically
store important documents, such as meeting minutes, membership
applications, and financial reports. The Vault, which is located within
the Member Center, allows officers to edit documents online, rather
than emailing them back and forth. This year, we enhanced The Vault’s
back-end architecture, making it more scalable and cost-effective for
lodges that need additional storage.
Another crucial function of our Member Services team is
administering registration for our statewide events. This year, the team
processed more than 6,000 event registrations for leadership retreats,
symposiums, conferences, the World Conference, and the Annual
Communication. During many events, they provided crucial handson support, including information and registration assistance, vendor
support, and concierge services.
Our leadership retreats had the highest attendance in years with
more than 1,000 participants. And, more than 500 Lodge Management
Certification Program courses were completed.
One of the biggest advances in Member Services this year was our
initiative to provide assistance to brothers around the state who desire
to create new lodges. As identified through the dialogue surrounding
the creation of the 2020 Plan, there has been tremendous interest in
new lodge development statewide. This year, groups of Masons have
expressed interest in creating 37 new lodges. Seven were granted
dispensations this year, 14 are making progress toward dispensation,
and 16 are preparing to submit a letter of intent.
Tomorrow, I will give a full report on charters, including a motion to
grant a new charter and one to accept a surrendered charter.
