Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents seek to amend the investments in which a lodge
may invest lodge funds.
Section 809.130 of the California Masonic Code on lodge
investments was most recently amended in 2008 and 2010 and currently
requires at least 20% of the lodge assets to be in short-term liquid
investments and up to 80% of the other assets may be in longer-term
specified investments.
This Resolution will allow lodges more flexibility by providing three
tiers of investments and adding and clarifying the types of investments.
Tier 1, known as Cash Reserves, will be the lesser of 8% of the
lodge’s assets or two times the lodge’s average annual expenditures over
the prior three full calendar years and must be invested in generally
liquid assets including cash, money market funds, checking and savings
accounts, certificates of deposit with maturities of less than two years,
and Obligations of the United States Government with maturities of
less than three years.
Tier 2, known as Fixed Income, will be the balance of the 20%
investment of the Tier 1 class, and in addition to the same Tier 1
investments, will include Certificates of Deposit and Obligations of
the United States Government without regard to maturity. Four other
types of investments are included as specified in the Resolution.

238

239

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Tier 3, known as Growth Assets, will be no more than 80% of the
lodge’s assets and may include Common Stocks, Preferred Stocks,
Master Limited Partnerships, Convertible Notes and Bonds, Convertible
Preferred Stocks, American Depository Receipts, and Real Estate
Investment Trusts.

Tier 3 “Growth Assets” are designed to provide for the longterm financial health of the lodge. These investments are intended to
ensure that future generations may continue to receive the benefits of
Masonry and to enable lodges to expand their capacity. The investment
options under Tier 3 have been increased to keep up with the current
investment world.

All three Tiers may use investment companies or investment trusts
that invest in the referenced financial classes.
Other prudent and appropriate investments for Tier 2 and Tier 3
classes may be approved from time to time by the Grand Master after
consultation with the Grand Treasurer and the Grand Lodge Committee
on Investments.
Last year Resolution 15-02 allowed lodges to transfer up to 80% of
lodge funds for investment with the Grand Lodge Constituent Lodge
Trust Fund. This Resolution reclassifies investments into three tiers
and requires only Tier 1 assets to be kept separate and not transferred
to that fund.
The impact of this legislation will depend upon a particular lodge’s
assets, investment strategy, and spending.
Report from the Investment Committee
This resolution is intended to enable lodges to balance their
operational funding needs with their long-term objectives, while
expanding acceptable investment alternatives. The character of some
allowed investments has changed, become ambiguous, or are patently
inappropriate, deeming clarification necessary.
This resolution defines three “tiers” of lodge investments and
elaborates on the investment guidelines. The first tier, “Cash Reserves,”
should cover two years of operating costs and is intended to ensure
sufficient liquidity for lodge operations. As is the case today, Tier 1
investments can only be held in only cash and equivalents, such as
insured CDs and money markets.
Tier 2 “Fixed Income” investments are expanded to include
investment options for medium-term needs and “just-in-case” funds.
This covers the remainder of the existing 20% tier as described in
CMC Section 809.130. It enables lodges to invest these funds in
anything defined in Tier 1 OR fixed income investments defined by
this resolution.

Resolution 16-08 creates new options and provides necessary
clarification, but does not require lodges to invest any differently than
they do today. The Committee on Investments believes this resolution
provides important updates to improve a lodge’s ability and choices to
prudently manage the funds entrusted to their care. We support and
recommend the adoption of resolution 16-08.
Resolution PASSED.

approved by a two-thirds affirmative vote of the
members present who are in good standing;
4.	
The Secretary of the lodge shall note in the minutes of
the lodge the notice of the proposed transaction when
made; and
C.	
Approved by the Committee on Masonic Properties as and to
the extent provided in Section 406.060 of this Code.
The lease of real property, as lessor or lessee, for no more than
three years shall not require member or shareholder approval under
clause B above.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
Proponents of this resolution seek to clarify the California Masonic
Code regarding obtaining lodge consent before a Masonic Hall
Association may sell its Masonic Hall.
California Corporations Code 1001 (a) states that “A corporation
may sell, lease, convey, exchange, transfer, or otherwise dispose of all
or substantially all of its assets when the principal terms are approved
by the board, and, unless the transaction is in the usual and regular
course of its business, approved by the outstanding shares (Section
152), either before or after approval by the board and before or after
the transaction.”

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

241

A lodge or group of lodges has the majority share of the Hall
Association. As a lodge consists of many members with equal voting
rights, clarification is needed to determine whether the lodge as a whole
shall give its consent for the sale of the Masonic Hall.
The particulars of this resolution include 15-day written notice to
all members of the details regarding the sale, as well as notification of
the date in which the lodge will vote. A two-thirds majority is required
by the lodge members present at the vote. Also this resolution re-states
(from CMC section 406.060) that the Committee on Masonic Properties
must approve the sale.
Leases of real property, less than three years, are excluded from the
proposed code. This provision is not present in carryover Resolution
15-01, which also addresses the issue of lodge approval of the sale of a
Masonic Hall. If both resolutions should pass, the one with the greater
vote takes effect.
This resolution ensures our practices as stated in the CMC are
consistent with California law. The voting process within the lodge for
such an approval is also consistent with CMC procedures for similar
processes. The proposed language appears to be appropriate for
clarifying and reinforcing proper procedures for the management of a
Masonic property.
Report from the Masonic Properties Committee
The proponents of Resolution 16-09 seek to clarify and establish a
procedure for lodge consent before a Masonic Hall Association may sell
its Masonic Hall.
The California Masonic Code allows a Masonic lodge to invest
funds in or maintain an investment in membership or shares in a
Masonic Hall Association wherein a lodge or lodges collectively hold a
majority interest.
California Non-profit Mutual Benefit Corporation Code Section
7011 provides: “a corporation may sell, lease, convey, exchange,
transfer, or otherwise dispose of all or substantially all of its assets
when the principal terms are: Approved by the board; and Unless the
transaction is in the usual and regular course of its activities, approved
by members.”

242

243

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Since all California Hall Associations are organized or should be
organized pursuant to California Non-profit Mutual Benefit Corporation
Code, Section 7011 is applicable to all such Hall Associations. Moreover,
since California Masonic Code requires majority interest by a lodge or
lodges (collectively) in Hall Associations, such Hall Associations cannot
dispose of their principal assets without the affirmative vote of the
majority interest.

WHEREAS, it is appropriate for the Code to be consistent with
regard to such membership matters.

Since California Masonic Code is silent respecting the procedure
by which consent of the lodge(s) is obtained, and since pursuant to the
Code and title requirement consent must be secured before sale of Hall
Association’s principal asset, this resolution sets forth and clarifies the
procedure through which such consent is to be obtained.
Resolution 16-09, in Section B (2) provides a 15-day written notice
requirement to each lodge member setting forth principal terms and
the date at which the vote for the sale of the property is to be taken.
Resolution 16-09 also clarifies that the lease of real property, as
lessor or lessee, for less than three years shall not require member or
shareholder approval.
The Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Properties supports
Resolution 16-09 and recommends a yes vote.
Resolution PASSED.

Resolution No. 16-10
Requires a Member to be in Good Standing
to Object to an Applicant
The proponents of this Resolution seek to require a member to be
in good standing in order to object to an applicant.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, a Master Mason must be in good standing in order to
vote upon applications for membership or affiliation; and
WHEREAS, the present Code does not use this same requirement
for the filing of an objection to election, initiation, or affiliation; and

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.510 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.510. OBJECTION BY A MEMBER BEFORE BALLOT.
At any time after an application for the degrees is received and
before the ballot, objection to the applicant’s election may be made
orally or in writing by any member Master Mason who is a member in
good standing of the lodge privately to the Master. No ballot shall be
taken unless the objection is withdrawn. The Investigating Committee
need not be appointed, or if appointed need not act, unless the objection
is withdrawn. If an objection is made, the Master shall report the fact to
the lodge at the next stated meeting. If the objection is made at a stated
meeting, the Master shall report the fact to the lodge at that meeting.
Unless the objection is withdrawn within 60 days of the stated meeting at
which it was reported by the Master, such objection shall have the effect
of a rejection by ballot and shall be reported to the Grand Secretary.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 804.520 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.520. OBJECTION BY A MEMBER BEFORE INITIATION.
If objection is made by any Master Mason who is a member in
good standing of the lodge to an applicant for the degrees is made after
election and before the initiation has been completed, the applicant
shall not receive the degree or the remainder thereof unless the
objection is withdrawn. If an objection is made, the Master shall report
the fact to the lodge at the next stated meeting. If the objection is made
at a stated meeting, the Master shall report the fact to the Lodge at
that meeting. Unless the objection is withdrawn within 60 days of the
stated meeting at which it was reported by the Master, such objection
shall have the effect of a rejection by ballot and shall be reported to
the Grand Secretary. No reason need be given for the objection, and it
may be renewed after withdrawal. [Source: Section 26240 of the 1991
California Masonic Code.]
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 804.530 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

244

Proceedings of the

§804.530. OBJECTION BY A MEMBER AFTER INITIATION.
If objection to advancement is made by any member Master Mason
who is a member in good standing of the lodge after the candidate’s
initiation, before being raised, the cause for the objection must be
stated. If no cause is stated, the Master may disregard the objection
and proceed to confer the remaining degree or degrees. If the cause
seems insufficient to the Master, he shall relate the matter to the lodge
at its next stated meeting, and the lodge shall then decide, by majority
vote, whether or not further investigation shall be made. If the objection
seems to the Master to be sufficient or to merit investigation, or if the
lodge shall so decide, the Master shall:
A.

Appoint a committee to inquire into the cause of the objection;

Fix the time and place for its meeting;

Have the objector and the applicant notified thereof; and

D.	

summoned to appear.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 804.560 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.560. OBJECTION BY A NON‑MEMBER.
A lodge must give immediate attention to a proper objection made
by another lodge, a Mason of any lodge or a non‑Mason to the election
for the degrees, initiation or advancement of an applicant or candidate.
The Master should appoint a committee to investigate and report on
the validity of the objection. If the committee determines that the
objection is proper and valid, proceedings should be taken as provided
for elsewhere in this Article as if the objection had been made by a
member Master Mason who is a member in good standing of the lodge.
If the committee determines that the objection is not proper and valid,
no further action is required.

§804.710. INVESTIGATING COMMITTEE.
An application for affiliation from an Entered Apprentice, a Fellow
Craft, or a Master Mason shall be balloted upon with no requirement
for investigation unless an objection is made by any member Master

At any time after an application for the affiliation is received and

the lodge at the next stated meeting. If the objection is made at a stated

which it was reported by the Master, such objection shall have the effect
of a rejection by ballot and shall be reported to the Grand Secretary.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to clarify how an objection to
an application or advancement of a candidate by an Entered Apprentice
or Fellow Craft Mason is resolved. Historically, any member of a lodge
may object to an application for membership or affiliation, or to the
advancement of a candidate. In recent years, there have been changes
to the definition of member as it relates to certain privileges.
When Resolution 11-06 was adopted in 2012, Entered Apprentice
and Fellow Craft Masons were allowed to attend lodge stated meetings.
This brought about a large number of changes to the California Masonic
Code. Many sections of the CMC have been updated to state that certain
privileges are restricted to Master Masons only. In the ensuing years,
additional changes have been made to the CMC to clarify and correct
additional sections. Resolution 11-13 required members to be in “good
standing” to be able to conduct lodge business.

246

Proceedings of the

This resolution clarifies how an objection to an application or
advancement of a candidate is resolved. If a Master Mason in Good
Standing objects, the application or advancement is suspended until the
objection is withdrawn. If a non-Mason, an Entered Apprentice, Fellow
Craft, or Master Mason not in good standing objects, the objection must
be investigated, and its validity reported.
Resolution PASSED.

Report of the Board of Trustees
Masonic Homes of California
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
For over 118 years, our Masonic Homes has stood as a safe haven
for the thousands of brothers, wives, widows, and orphans who have
made their way up our front steps to find a place of brotherly love and
relief. In 1898, brothers began coming to our campus in Decoto to find
respite. More than a century later, that same spirit of relief can be found
at our residential campuses in Covina and Union City, at our Masonic
Center for Youth and Families (MCYAF), and in the communities we
serve through Masonic Outreach Services (MOS). The Masonic Homes
ensures that our brothers and their wives and widows are never without
the resources they need to age successfully.
We continue to make a profound difference in the lives of the
members we serve and we often hear that Masonic Homes residents
have just one regret – that they didn’t come sooner. This year we served
more than 350 residents at our residential communities in Union City
and Covina, at the skilled nursing, assisted living, and independent
living levels of care. Our skilled nursing facility in Union City continued
to maintain a coveted five-star rating from Medicare. Much has
changed over the years in the way we care for our elderly brothers,
but our commitment to excellence continues to be the hallmark of the
Masonic Homes.
Our Masonic Assistance line, (888) 466-3642, continues to be the
single point of entry for all of the services provided through the Masonic
Homes. This number is printed on the back of every dues card for easy
reference. Last year, we handled more than 2,052 calls.
Changes in membership demographics have called for us to take
new approaches in the way that we provide relief. Our brothers and
their widows are living longer, and life expectancies will continue to rise
with advances in medicine. Quality of life measures are also improving,
as people are remaining active longer. Our 100 Plus Club continues to
grow; this year, we had more residents over age 100 than ever before.

250

251

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

By providing care management and direct financial assistance, MOS
allows brothers and their wives or widows to successfully age in place,
close to their lodges, families, and friends. Our MOS program continues
to grow as more and more aging brothers are in need of assistance.
Last year, MOS served 357 clients, a six percent increase over 2015.
The majority of those clients received direct financial assistance, while
others received ongoing case management.

In summer 2015, we opened Transitions, a new short-term
rehabilitation and respite program in the newly renovated third floor
of the Lorber skilled nursing facility in Union City. Transitions offers
private rooms, a dining room with menu service, and state-of-the art
rehabilitation equipment. It provides specialized care for cardiac,
orthopedic, and neurosurgical rehabilitation, as well as transitional care
for patients needing short-term stays. This new program was the result
of more than 18 months of planning with the local health care system
in the Tri-City area.

Unfortunately, along with longer life expectancies and medical
advancements come higher costs. Many brothers, and, especially,
widows aren’t able to afford basic necessities, let alone the high cost of
medical care. It is estimated that 20 percent of those over 75 live below
the poverty level. With wait lists still averaging over 18-24 months for
our residential communities, MOS is working hard to provide care in
brothers’ own communities. But for those wanting to be among their
brothers, 18-24 months is too long to wait.
This year, we continued to embrace change while moving forward
with our strategic plan, “Roadmap 2020.” Begun at our 2014 February
board retreat, Roadmap 2020 is guiding us in improving care on our
campuses and in our communities. Our goal is to reduce waitlists,
provide all needed levels of care, and be there for our brothers and
widows at their time of need. You can see these goals reflected in the
many new programs offered by the Masonic Homes this year.
The Lodge Outreach Program began in 2012. This has been an
excellent initiative for educating members about Masonic Assistance,
extending Masonic relief, and engaging members in a meaningful
way, while positioning the Masonic Homes to better meet the needs of
our diverse membership. We are completing the rollout of the Lodge
Outreach Program and hope to be operational in all Divisions by
March 2017.
Thanks to a direct-admit program for skilled nursing care that we
started this year, the Masonic Homes is now able to accept members at
any level of care – independent living, assisted living, or skilled nursing.
A brother, wife, or widow in need of skilled nursing can now be admitted
directly into our Union City community for this greatly needed service.

Our Stepping Stones Program addresses the ever-changing needs
of residents suffering from memory loss or cognitive impairment from
Alzheimer’s or other forms of dementia. This new approach, which
provides a continuum of care, is based upon our understanding that
memory loss is a progressive illness that requires different approaches
at different stages. We partnered with experts in the field of cognitive
health to create the Brain Gym, where residents can exercise their
minds with the latest in computer stimulation.
Our Compass Club program is the first of its kind and has gained
national attention. An alternative to a traditional social day program,
it provides a cost-effective solution to the growing need for caregiver
respite, as well as a structured environment for those suffering from
mild cognitive impairment. This year, we were honored to present the
Compass Club at the California LeadingAge Annual Conference. As a
result, two communities have replicated the program and we can now
work together to effect improvements.
Our Traditions program continues to provide assisted living in
a safe environment with specialized programing for residents whose
needs cannot be met in our independent living or other assisted living
units. The memory care unit at Lorber completes our Stepping Stones
program by providing skilled nursing for those suffering from more
acute medical needs in addition to dementia.
Through our development of memory care programs such as
the ones described here, we making a difference in the communities
we serve, having a profound impact on thousands of Masons and
non-members.

252

253

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

The Masonic Homes has been helping children for more than 100
years. Today, MCYAF continues this heritage by providing professional,
integrated therapeutic services for youth who struggle with behavioral,
learning, and mental health difficulties. Located in San Francisco,
MCYAF serves Masonic and non-Masonic children throughout the
state. This fall, MCYAF will expand to a second location on the Covina
campus to provide therapeutic support to Southern California children.

of life for our residents. Sixteen neighborhoods will be built around a
shared kitchen, living room, and dining room, giving residents a greater
sense of “home,” as opposed to an institutional feel.

As part of our ongoing effort to acquaint all of our brothers with the
Masonic Homes, our Union City campus hosted its second HarvestFest
in October 2015. Rainbow Road was dedicated as part of the celebration
and Job’s Daughter’s Lane was dedicated in May 2016. More than 1,000
of our brothers and their families attended these events.
This year marked the centennial of our Covina Masonic Home.
Nearly 2,000 people came to Covina to celebrate 100th anniversary
of our Southern California campus. Surrounded by the historic midcentury modern architecture, we were treated to a day of food and fun.
Once you’ve had a chance to visit one of our campuses, you will be
forever changed. You will be proud of what we have accomplished so
far, and how we continue to make a profound difference in the lives of
those in need.
The future for our Masonic Homes remains bright.
Our campus master planning process formed the basis of a plan
to replace aging facilities on our Union City campus and to add new
facilities that will allow us to provide much-needed skilled nursing and
memory care services in Covina.
In Union City, the existing Lorber skilled nursing building is based
on an outdated model of care that doesn’t allow us to follow current best
practices. Several additional factors, including a shortage of parking
and state building restrictions, have created challenges for improving
other structures on campus. Plans are now underway to replace Lorber
with a new 96-bed health center. This state-of-the art skilled nursing
facility will be constructed in a neighborhood model, allowing for
maximum flexibility in caring for those in need of memory care, shortterm rehabilitation, long-term care, or assisted living. Private rooms,
with private baths and showers, will significantly improve the quality

In Covina, the lack of programs and services due to a lack of
facilities has challenged our ability to provide a full continuum of care
in Southern California. Covina residents are currently “outplaced”
if they need skilled nursing or memory care, separating spouses and
making visits difficult. We have less ability to monitor the quality of
care and service in these outside facilities. To address these challenges,
a new 32-bed, state-of-the-art health center is being planned to bring
much-needed skilled nursing and memory care to Covina. No longer
will spouses be separated, or will our brothers or their widows have to
leave our Masonic community to get care elsewhere.
Also in Covina, we are repurposing two of the former children’s
homes for clients of our MOS program. These unused houses are being
converted to 14 senior housing units – a mix of bedrooms and suites.
They will provide greatly needed housing for MOS clients, many of
whom have been waiting more than a year to enter our Covina
Masonic Home. Featuring an elevator and common areas, they are an
ideal solution for our independent brethren and widows needing an
affordable place to call home.
These new programs and services on both campuses will improve
quality of life for our members and decrease waiting lists. No longer will
brothers have to wait years for admission; we will be able to better take
care of brothers and their wives or widows who are vulnerable, in need,
and who want to age among brethren.
Your generous support of the Annual Fund and through planned
giving ensures that we can continue to meet the increasing and diverse
needs of our most vulnerable members.
We are forever grateful for the generosity that has given us the
opportunity to make such a profound difference in the lives of our
brothers and their wives and widows, as well as the children that we
serve. Generations of Masons gave of their time and resources to make
our Masonic Homes what it is today and it is our mission to preserve
that legacy for generations yet to come.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
Acacia Creek, our continuing care retirement community located
adjacent to the Masonic Home at Union City, is now in its sixth year
of operation. I am pleased to report to you that we have achieved
100% occupancy at the community. At the time of the last Annual
Communication our occupancy was at 83%. Our marketing program is
now refocused on expanding the Master Wait List in order to develop
prospects ready to quickly move in when a transition occurs. The
community continues to meet the 25-year pro forma and will begin
making payments on our debt.
This year, Acacia Creek applied for and received our permanent
Certificate of Authority from the California Department of Social
Services, which is our license to sell CCRC apartments - another
significant milestone. The community also received approval from the
department for the additional licensing of the last 39 apartments which
had been suspended since the opening. The community also completed
its five-year survey by the department with no citations or notes
of deficiencies.
Current residents’ satisfaction and happiness is apparent to
prospective buyers, and because of this our residents continue to be our
best salespeople in the community and are always involved in the sales
process as we continue to build the Master Wait List. Residents invite
friends and lodge brothers to join them for meals or for an overnight stay
in the guest apartments, and “host” them for dinner and entertainment.
Masterpiece Living is a national program of physical and mental
wellness which has been adopted by Acacia Creek to support our
philosophy of successful aging. Measured against the national
benchmarks for residents in similar communities, our residents again
this year showed a lower level of physical problems and a higher level of
nutritional and physical activity. To this end, during 2015 Acacia Creek
constructed an annex connected to the Wellness Center to provide
expanded space for exercise classes.

270

271

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

The absorption of non-Masons into the Acacia Creek community
has been rewarding for the Fraternity. There is great camaraderie among
them and the community has been strengthened by adding to the mix.
Nine residents have become Master Masons since opening, and more
are expected to petition for degrees in the future. Members of Acacia
Creek are actively involved with Siminoff Daylight Lodge No. 850 at the
Masonic Home at Union City as members, officers, and in building and
maintaining the new outdoor degree site on the property. One of our
residents recently received the Hiram Award for outstanding service to
the Siminoff Lodge and the fraternity.

I want to thank the members of the Grand Lodge Executive
Committee, the Grand Lodge staff, the Masonic Homes Board of
Trustees, and the Acacia Creek Board for their expertise, their vision,
and their passion. Together we look forward to continuing the mission
of bringing Acacia Creek to financial security and a successful future.

The Acacia Creek staff continues to share feedback about the
positive work environment they enjoy through the team management
concept. Employees are decision-makers and feel a sense of ownership
in the operations of Acacia Creek. This results in a very low turnover
among staff, adding to the comfort level of the residents.
When the fraternity planned the Acacia Creek community, we
envisioned that it would include all levels of health care, including
independent and assisted living, skilled nursing, and memory care.
To fulfill this goal, Acacia Creek has worked with the Masonic Homes
in designing the renovation of the Traditions Program of the Masonic
Home at Union City, and the planning of the Campus Master Plan which
will create new opportunities for expanded services on the campus,
including the development of a short-term rehab center and a unique
dementia skilled nursing program, which were opened during 2015.
The Masonic Homes Board and the Acacia Creek Board continue
to collaborate on improvements and new facilities on the Union City
campus. Ongoing discussions continue regarding the expansion of
methods of serving the needs of our prospective clients over the long
term and further improving the lives of our current residents.
The board wishes to extend our sincere appreciation to Acacia Creek
Executive Vice President Chuck Major, who has been responsible for
the high level of morale and accountability of the staff and the strategic
Marketing Program that has brought Acacia Creek to 100% occupancy.

Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F&A.M. of California:
Your California Masonic Foundation continued its focus this year on
our two primary program areas – elementary school literacy and college
access. Through our partnerships with Raising A Reader, as well as
several college access organization programs statewide, we continue to
affect the lives of the children whose educational futures are often most
at risk. The successful work of our Public Schools Advisory Councils has
continued to foster important relationships in our communities. These
brethren organize Public Schools Month events, interview Investment
in Success scholarship candidates and help celebrate public education
in eight regions across the state. Masons Night was, once again,
celebrated in Major League ballparks in San Diego, Los Angeles, and San
Francisco. The captains of our Masons 4 Mitts teams spread excitement
and enthusiasm in these regions for our collaborative efforts to help
improve our communities.
Strategic Initiatives
Our aim is to support public education and increase opportunities
for lodges to engage their communities. Our Public Schools Advisory
Councils organized eight Public Schools Month celebrations in April
2016. Public Schools Month events were attended by more than 500
people - including 327 Masons. At each event, Masonic brothers, school
district staff, teachers, parents, students, and community members
celebrated our charitable investment.This year, the fraternity’s statewide
support of California’s public schools had two primary components; the
award-winning child literacy and family engagement program Raising
A Reader and the innovative Investment in Success Scholarship. These
very successful celebrations further raised community awareness of
Freemasonry and demonstrated our dedication to both public education
and the lifelong learning of our students.
Our efforts acknowledge and support the critical role that families
and networks play in a student’s ability to succeed. Whether they are
kindergartners or high school seniors – we know that adding a few key
ingredients can make all the difference in their lives. To that end, we
have engaged in partnerships, developed programs and encouraged our

Public Schools Advisory Councils (PSACs)
As a fraternity, our greatest strength lies in our members. Through
our PSACs, the Foundation is able to maximize our impact by engaging
key leaders and leveraging partnerships with organizations that share
our values and strategic objectives. By working with our members and
partners to ensure the success of Raising A Reader and guaranteeing
that our Investment in Success recipients have a college success
organization supporting them throughout, we provide the necessary
combination of financial support and wraparound services needed for
students to achieve academically, and complete college. In addition, our
PSACs allow us to expand our impact beyond our program participants
and scholarship beneficiaries as we collaborate in creating additional
resources that are accessible to families statewide.
PSACs are located in areas with high concentrations of California
Masons where we have built relationships with local public
school districts.

This year, 58 of our brethren were members of these councils. They
are the “boots on the ground” in our efforts to connect our work to
education and community leaders, families and students.
At each of these Public Schools Month events, which were held at
schools in districts implementing the Raising A Reader program, our
Grand Master highlighted our support for public education; thanked
district leaders, teachers and parents for their important roles; and
presented a total of$900,000 to support Raising A Reader and Investment
in Success in these communities. Each council performed admirably

274

Proceedings of the

and worked closely with the Grand Lodge staff to assure successful
celebratory events. The councils played a key role in soliciting local
lodges to help raise money to bring Raising A Reader to new classrooms
in their regions of California.
In addition, the councils conducted the Investment in Success
scholarship interview and selection process. Since 2011, the
Councils have interviewed more than 600 students - recommending
366 for scholarships. Personal presentations of the scholarship
awards were made when possible to further highlight the students’
accomplishments while publicly reinforcing the Fraternity’s
commitment to public education.
The Foundation Board of Trustees thanks each member of our
Public Schools Advisory Councils. You are critical to implementing
our investments in public education, whether you are raising funds,
interviewing students or planning an event - you are the keys to our
success. We are humbled by, and extremely proud of, your tireless
efforts on behalf of the Foundation.
Elementary School Literacy
We are pleased to continue our successful partnership with
Raising A Reader (RAR), a national leader in child literacy and family
engagement thinking. As of this Annual Communication, the program
is active in 117 California schools in 30 different school districts,
encompassing 448 classrooms. This is an amazing accomplishment,
and we congratulate all of the lodges and brethren who have helped
make this possible. Nearly 40,000 children and families have had the
benefit of RAR as a result of our fraternity’s charitable investments in
California’s elementary schools.
The aim of our work with RAR is to install the program in California
classrooms most at risk of academic failure. Each academic year, 100
high-quality, professionally-chosen books are distributed to each
family. By 2020, the Masons of California will have brought the gift of
reading to more than 50,000 children and their families. The positive
response from parents, educators, and leaders across the state also
increases the overall awareness of Freemasonry as a force for good in
our communities.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

275

Teacher of the Year
The Foundation continued its major sponsorship this year of the
California Teacher of the Year program. The annual state banquet was
held in Sacramento in February and the five Teacher of the Year finalists
were recognized. The Grand Master also presented a$1,000 check to
each of the five finalists. The five were also honored at a celebration
within their own communities and received special gifts from the
Foundation. The Foundation also gave$250 stipends to the six finalists
and eight semi-finalists.
Investment in Success
We take scholarships very seriously. Our goal is that every
scholarship dollar invested in a student’s future has the potential to
change a life forever. With Investment in Success, now completing its
fifth year, we have continued to answer this challenge. This year, 95
new young people received a scholarship from the Foundation that few
of them ever dreamed possible. The scholarship dollars, amounting to
more than$400,000, will change the lives of the more than 300 students
currently enrolled in our program.
The Investment in Success scholarship is awarded to that student
attempting to overcome many of life’s challenges and obstacles to
achieve his or her academic dreams. Nearly all are first-in-family to
attend college and have little or no resources – yet all have demonstrated
a powerful desire to succeed, a vision for their future, the commitment
to better themselves and to give back to their communities. The
Foundation has structured this program to allow for the realities of their
lives. We have a more flexible structure, which acknowledges time and
family commitments. We provide summer school funding, and support
our students in every way we can.
This year, for the first time, we developed partnerships with college
success organizations in each of our eight PSAC regions. These college
success organizations, who nominate students with whom they are
working for our scholarship, ensure that our Investment in Success
students receive financial aid, academic advising, and specialized
support services throughout their high school and college careers –
thus increasing their chances of graduation and success.

Youth Order Grants
A key priority of our Grand Master, M. David Perry, was the creation
of a scholarship that would support youth order leaders. Thanks
to the leadership of our Grand Master, and with the support of the
Executive Committee, the Foundation, in conjunction with the Youth
Orders Committee, created the Masonic Youth Leadership Scholarship,
designed to recognize and support youth leaders of our four youth
orders. Twenty-two members of our Masonic Youth Orders received a
scholarship of$3,000 each to help fund their college education. We are
proud to be able to support these amazing young people.
Other Programs
The Foundation continued this year to underwrite our existing
leadership development, lodge growth, and Masonic education
programs; including the Masters and Wardens Leadership Retreats,
Lodge Certification Program, Inspectors’ Development Academy,
Masonic Formation, the Institute for Masonic Studies and the Masonic
Symposium. In addition, our heritage sites, historic article preservation,
Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum, and California Masonic
Memorial Temple maintenance were funded.
Board Governance
The Board of Trustees continued to function within the governance
model adopted three years ago across all the constitutional boards. The
Foundation continues to operate and meet the reporting requirements
of the model, with constant, longer term, strategic planning discussions
encompassed by the Ends Policy of the Board. The board also focused
on succession planning, to assure that appropriate leadership talent is
brought to the Foundation over the next strategic plan period.
Looking Forward to 2017
The Foundation will enter the coming year with a focus on the
fraternity’s next five-year plan. With the 2020 strategic plan of the
Masons of California will come new challenges to be addressed. We
will continue to monitor the classrooms receiving Raising a Reader and
involve even more of our lodge members in the activities of the Public
Schools Advisory Councils. We will further refine our Investment in
Success program to increase the number of students with whom we can
make a profound difference through access to higher education.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

277

The board will also prepare to implement the new thrusts of the
strategic plan assigned to the Foundation. Currently, the board is actively
participating in the major review of our fraternity’s philanthropy and
fundraising approaches as documented in the Mitchell study conducted
this year. The Foundation anticipates an evolving role in the changes to
this critical area over the next several years. Lastly, we will continue
to work toward increasing our financial resources in order to have a
significantly greater impact on society by our 50th anniversary in 2019.
Acknowledgements
The Trustees wish to thank Most Worshipful Perry for our
appointments and the opportunity to serve this Grand Lodge. Special
thanks in particular go to the Grand Lodge staff led by Very Worshipful
Allan Casalou, Grand Secretary, for their continued outstanding
leadership, guidance, and support to this Foundation Board of Trustees.

Respectfully submitted,

Report of the Board of Trustees of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple

We again hope that the brethren will make it a point to visit
the California Masonic Memorial Temple on Nob Hill when in San
Francisco and take advantage of the collections of the Henry Wilson
Coil Library and Museum, view the endomosaic mural designed and
constructed by Emile Norman, and attend the variety of concerts held
in the auditorium.

Following last year’s Annual Communication, we hosted the XIV
World Conference of Regular Grand Lodges from November 18-21, a
rare opportunity to showcase the best of California Masonic hospitality
and scholarship. The CMMT hosted the welcoming reception in front of
our Masonic endomosaic mural in the foyer of the building. We will refer
you to the Grand Master’s report on the successful event that exposed
the building to brothers from many countries around the world.
CMMT operations remain stable and positive eight months into
the fiscal year. Live Nation remains a good tenant and partner. They
have expressed satisfaction with their business here. They continue to
book and manage high-quality concerts and have brought high-quality
corporate events to the building. In addition to many nationally known
music artists, a number of “celebrities” have appeared in the building
this year including Hillary Clinton and Anderson Cooper.
Financial performance has been strong and predictable. 2016
represents the first year CMMT will finish with an operational surplus
after depreciation expense in a very long time. Total positive cash flow
for the year is forecasted to be$324,000 compared to budgeted positive
cash flow of$309,000; again, one of our best years in decades.
We are working to develop a new five-year capital plan for
additional improvements. Other than the third-floor renovation, the
capital expenditures incurred this year were minor replacements. The
ADA improvements and the study that were done in 2014 and 2015
were finally completed and booked in 2016. Over the last 18 months,
we have researched cogeneration, which could be a viable option for
CMMT to realize significant savings in utility costs. For the time being,
we are putting the cogeneration project on hold while we focus on the
installation of Nob Hill solar system, which will be completed during
the next quarter. We will resume the cogeneration discussion in 2017.
Neighborhood relations continue to be important to us and are
very good. We have hosted two of four Nob Hill Community Liaison
Group meetings this year. No reports of neighbor complaints have been
received this year. We held another CMMT building tour for the Nob
Hill neighborhood on August 30. We are also organizing a Nob Hill
Night Out for the neighborhood in conjunction with the Il Divo concert
on November 13.

The board wishes to extend its gratitude to our executive vice
president and Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, our Chief Financial
Officer Thomas J. Boyer, and Khalil Sweidy, Director of Financial
Planning, and especially their respective staff who work so diligently in
representing our interests, and maintaining and managing the building.
We also thank the grand master, Most Worshipful David M. Perry for the
opportunity to serve, and for his active support and faith in our efforts.
Respectfully submitted,
Mark E. Pressey, President
William J. Bray III, Vice President

Report of the Board of Trustees of the
Nob Hill Masonic Center
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California F &A M,
The NHMC Board is happy to present this annual report informing
the membership of this Grand Lodge of the ongoing activities and
operations for managing the garage at Grand Lodge of California
Masonic Temple at 1111 California St. in San Francisco. As the NHMC
Board is the only “for-profit” board among all of the constitutional Grand
Lodge Boards, our primary Ends Policy is to oversee the profitable
operation of the garage which will render a minimum predetermined
Dividend to its stakeholder, The Grand Lodge of California F&AM.
This year, your board is happy to report that ongoing operations of
the garage will continue to generate a profit and ultimately resulting in
the board being able to pay the Grand Lodge a dividend in the amount
of$380,000. to help fund the GL operations. With the completion of the
upgrade to the Temple and the garage behind us, Live Nation continues
to lease out the building for more large and small events, which generates
event parking revenue. Ace Parking will continue to seek out additional
sources of revenue, over and above our current sources, namely, Zipcar
and Get-around. We are continuing efforts to grow daily and monthly
parking as well off-hour parking during the night/morning hours when
the garage is not fully parked.
The successful management of the garage operations is directly
attributable to the effective leadership of our Executive Vice President,
Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, and with the expertise of our CFO, Tom
Boyer and his staff. The Board is thankful for their continued efforts
transacting the business of the garage for the betterment of our Craft.
The year, the board will be reviewing the Ace Parking Management
contract which is up for renewal this year, measuring their performance
based on preceeding years’ results and efforts to increase the garage
capacity as outlined in their Service Contract. Ace will continue to seek
out new sources of revenue for the garage to supplement contracts with
car-sharing services, such as Zipcar, and Get-around.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

281

New Improvements to the garage this year:
In our continuing efforts to increase profitability of the garage and
minimize overall costs, the old fluorescent bulbs in the garage have
been replaced with new LED lighting.
Second, a new parking automation system, including software and
equipment was installed in order to meet the demands of increased
parking and the ability to handle online pre-parking reservations for
guests attending events at the building.
Lastly, in conjunction with the new lighting, and to further reduce
energy costs, solar energy panels will be installed on the roof. The
reduced energy costs, coupled with the depreciation and tax credits all
help the bottom line and ensuring our ability to continue to pay the
Grand Lodge a dividend for years to come. I would like to take this
opportunity to acknowledge the excellent work of Tom Boyer and his
staff for researching the vendors, system and equipment, as well as his
excellent negotiating skills.
It truly has been an honor to serve this GL as the President of the
NHMC Board this year and to work with such a fine group of Board
of Directors, VP Jeffrey Wilkins, MW Harry Maynard, John Nolan and
Frank Young. I would like to thank MW David Perry for his continued
support in allowing us to continue the work of our Craft and for this
masonic board.
Respectfully Submitted,
Garrett S. Chan, President

Report of the Committee
on Insurance
Overview
The Insurance committee is tasked with the responsibility of
reviewing the Grand Lodge property and casualty insurance program
and other related insurance programs, working with the broker selected
by Grand Lodge and making recommendations regarding coverage and
other insurance related matters. The Insurance Committee reports to
the Grand Secretary on all insurance matters (except Life and Medical
Coverage and benefits for employees) who then makes the final decision
regarding the different coverages and limits to purchase or renew. The
committee also works closely with the Chief Financial Officer on an
ongoing basis.
Currently there are three meetings a Masonic year of the full
Committee and an additional meeting in December for just the
Chairman, Vice Chairman, the CFO, other Grand Lodge representatives
and the Insurance Broker. The purpose of this meeting is to advise the
broker of any changes in Grand Lodge activities or new programs being
contemplated or under way. The broker provides any information on
changes in the insurance market place regarding cost, coverage and
availability. The broker may also make new recommendations regarding
insurance program. The date for the renewal quotes for the new policy
year is also set at this meeting.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Overview
The Investment Committee has been charged with the prudent
handling of Grand Lodge investment funds. These funds consist
primarily of the general and endowment funds for the Masonic Homes
of California, but also include the investment portfolios of the California
Masonic Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple, the Grand
Lodge retirement plan, and the Grand Lodge itself. We take this charge
very seriously. In its simplest terms, we manage the investment funds
with an eye to grow and preserve capital. We strive to maintain an
increasingly diversified portfolio that is designed to generate the
necessary funds for the continuing operation of Masonic functions, as
well as allow for growth for future needs. In doing so, we constantly
scan the horizon in an attempt to manage the funds to take advantage of
long-term trends as well as near-term opportunities. The Grand Lodge
Investment Committee utilizes the services of professional investment
management firms to gain access to the capital markets. The funds are
invested in the domestic United States, international equity markets,
fixed income markets, and alternative strategies which are not as
correlated to the traditional stock and bond markets.
The past year (ending June 30, 2016) yielded a negative return
on the invested funds. We recognize that not all years can be positive
years, and we remain committed to the process and to the structure of
the portfolio as constructed. We have spent a good deal of time finding
ways to balance risk and reward in the portfolio, and we have paid
special attention to the fact that fixed income (a traditional diversifier
to equity risk) has entered into a new economic cycle within the current
interest rate environment. To that end, the committee has implemented
several changes in recent years, including allocation to assets in the
“alternatives” category. While “alternatives” can be interpreted with
varying meanings, we use the term as a class of assets that seek
“absolute returns” independent of the movements in the stock and
bond markets. We expect that these allocations will provide important
diversification away from the risks that affect the stock market, while
delivering performance beyond that of bonds.

290

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Grand Lodge & Related Entity Investment Performance
For the year ended June 30, 2016

Summary of Recent Changes

The total Grand Lodge and related entities portfolio retracted
2.6 percent for the year ending June 30, 2016. The total fund policy
benchmark was up 1.2 percent and the consumer price index for the
year was 1.0 percent. The market value of the total Grand Lodge and
related entities portfolio as of June 30, 2016, was$846.6 million compared
to$901.9 million a year earlier. For the three-year period ending June
30, 2016, the combined Grand Lodge and related entities returned 4.6
percent versus 6.9 percent for the benchmark. Since inception, our
funds have returned 7.4 percent annually versus 7.6 percent return of
the benchmark.
The U.S. equity allocation of the portfolio was down 1.8 percent
compared to +2.0 percent for the Dow Jones Total Stock Market Index.
The Non-U.S. equity portfolio was down 2.9 percent compared to
-10.2 percent for the MSCI All Country World ex-U.S. Index. Global
Equities was down 10.1 percent compared to -3.7 percent for the
MSCI All-Country World Index. The fixed income portfolio was up 3.9
percent, compared to a 5.8 percent return for the fixed income custom
benchmark. our alternative investments were down 1.3 percent versus
+4.9 percent for the custom alternatives index. A more detailed manager
performance review can be found in the tables following this report.
The Investment Committee does not attempt to take advantage of
perceived short-term anomalies in the markets by chasing the most
recent top-performing asset class. Rather, it arrives at its recommended
allocation to stocks and bonds and other asset classes only after very
careful due diligence and consideration. The purpose of the funds, their
spending requirements, investment time horizon and ability to assume
risk are all factored into these recommendations. The probability and
duration of potential losses are carefully weighed against the long-term
potential for appreciation of assets after withdrawals are taken into
account. The Investment Committee recommends asset allocations that
will provide the highest probability that the funds will be able to meet
their respective objectives over the long term.
All returns are net of fees. Detailed entity performance can be found
in the tables following this report.

291

Over the past five years, the asset allocation for Grand Lodge
and related entities asset allocation has evolved in an effort to better
position the portfolio to withstand downturns in the market while still
maintaining the overall expected return. As such, we have progressed
from a traditional 60 percent equity/ 40 percent fixed income strategy to
one that incorporates more alternative asset classes. The current asset
allocation includes approximately 55 percent in public equities and 15
percent in fixed income. The remaining 30 percent of capital allocated
to alternative strategies is designed to perform well when the public
equity market struggles, thereby smoothing out the inevitable “ups and
downs” of the markets.
The fixed income portfolio continues to be managed in an
“unconstrained” manner. This means that the investment manager
has the ability to position the portfolio to withstand a rising interest
rate environment. When interest rates increase, bond prices decrease.
Utilizing the skills of a bond manager with multiple tools at their
disposal can minimize the damage of a rising interest rate environment
on a bond portfolio.
Grand Lodge Investment Management
For the year ended June 30, 2016
In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand
Lodge investment policy and philosophy, the Investment Committee
meets quarterly with our investment consultant, AON. We also meet
with our individual portfolio managers frequently (at least once every 18
months, but more frequently if they fall onto our watch list). We review
their respective performance compared to various indices representing
their objective. This process provides the Investment Committee with
the necessary data to evaluate each investment manager on a timely
basis, and to observe whether they continue to achieve the objectives
of their mandate.
The committee also holds monthly WebEx conference calls to
discuss any outstanding business, or discuss the implementation of
tactical changes within the portfolio.

292

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Proceedings of the

In addition, the committee makes regular calls to the managers
to assess if there have been any material changes at the respective
investment company that may affect the management of assets, or that
may be a sign of bigger potential issues that requires further review
and analysis.
Finally, we have scheduled bi-annual retreats to take time to review
our overall strategic initiatives implemented over the prior two years,
review the macro environment and opportunities therein and chart a
course for the following two-year period.
Our investment consultant, AON, has served us well over the years.
However, we recognize that due diligence is important, not only for
our managers but also for those providing advice and guidance on our
manager selection and overall strategic planning. To this end, a great
deal of time and energy has gone into a due diligence review of our
current consulting relationship, which includes a RFP process to gauge
services and pricing from other consulting firms in the marketplace.
That review process is nearly complete, and we will be reporting on
those results in next year’s report.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee is also available to assist
individual lodges in determining appropriate investment strategy.
One available vehicle to aid in this effort is the “Lodge Investment
Options Program” which is intended to assist lodges in determining
an appropriate investment strategy and asset allocation. Whether you
currently have lodge investments or are considering implementing
such a program, we direct your lodge trustees’ or investment committee
members’ attention to the Member Center website for more information
on this turnkey program. We are also here to help lodges establish a
set of policies and procedures that are designed to ensure assets are
invested according to the needs of the lodge and to safeguard against
the misuse of funds. Investment Committee members continue to make
themselves available to the lodges for assistance with this program and
other questions regarding lodge investments.

295

Report of the Committee
on Jurisprudence
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the
Grand Master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session.
The Committee reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations
to be considered at the next Annual Communication and prepares
any necessary legislation to carry out the intent of the proponents.
At the Annual Communication, it comments on the legality of the
Grand Master’s decisions and dispensations and on the legal effect
of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code
to reflect the legislation which was adopted.
In the Committee’s view, those of Grand Master Perry’s decisions
and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within
his discretion. In the Committee’s view, the legislation posted by the
Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge website on August 2 of this year is
sufficient to carry out the intent of the proponents, and the legislation
contained in Grand Master Perry’s recommendations which he will
present in his message is sufficient to carry out his intent. We believe
that each piece of this legislation has the legal effect set forth in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no
recommendations as to the action you should take with it. While the
Committee has written the title and introductory explanation for each
resolution before you and assisted the proponents in drafting the Code
changes required to effect their intent, the proponents’ arguments in
their whereas clauses are their own. The Committee does not assist in
drafting the whereas clauses and makes no comments on them.
The legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge
website on August 2 of this year and the legislation contained in
Grand Master Perry’s recommendations require no separate motion
because they are automatically before this Annual Communication.
The presiding officer will announce the vote required for the passage of
each item before discussion begins. Any legislation which does not
amend the Code or the Ritual requires a simple majority only for
adoption. Any amendment to the Code or the Ritual must be adopted
by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment receives a simple

296

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries over to the
next Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative vote is
required for adoption.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & AM of California
The Committee on Lodge Support is very thankful to be entrusted
with the opportunity by the Grand Master to serve the brethren and the
lodges of California this year.
With the realignment of districts, the 13 very dedicated brethren
of the Committee on Lodge Support have seen increased engagement
over previous years by having assisted more than 20 lodges in various
needs during this year. The members of the committee have generously
spent countless hours meeting with and traveling to these lodges to
help meet those needs - often competing with family, professional, and
fraternal responsibilities. Several situations required the committee to
help the brethren of a lodge alleviate an unfortunate circumstance and
stabilize the lodge for the benefit of continued Freemasonry in their
community. Fortunately, most of our efforts were focused at assisting
the brethren of lodges to develop or rekindle programs and best
practices that embrace Masonic values and enrich the lives of their
lodge members and the communities that each lodge serves. Although
one lodge has decided that they could not rebuild at this time and
have therefore surrendered their charter and one other lodge is in
the process of consolidation, most of the remaining lodges are making
progress toward improvement, with only a few still struggling to find
their way forward. On the whole, the committee has thankfully achieved
successes in all areas and is pleased to report that lodges requesting
assistance are generally moving in a positive direction.
The Committee on Lodge Support continues to believe that the
successful lodge will utilize a “best practice” approach to focus on four
major areas for growth, relevance, and success:
1. An engaging membership experience whereby each Mason
feels rewarded for being a part of our Craft.
2. Active community partnership and involvement whereby our
individual communities, and society in general, are beneficiaries
of Freemasonry.

298

Proceedings of the

3. Assisting each lodge to operate in a smooth and sound manner,
financially and administratively.
4. Promote methods that develop lodge leadership.
Through our interactions with individual lodges – and to prevent
or reduce the severity of a number of the crises we see – there are
five basic principles that can set a lodge on the trajectory to meet this
growth, relevance, and success:
1. Realize that success is not by accident; it must be encouraged,
enacted, and emphasized.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

299

The Committee on Lodge Support looks forward to assisting lodges
at the invitation of the individual lodge or its Master, at the request of the
Inspector or Assistant Grand Lecturer, or at the direction of the Grand
Master or the Executive Committee through mentoring and coaching.
The goal for each engagement is through the prism of the Grand
Lodge 2020 Fraternity Plan to expand and strengthen Freemasonry in
individual communities and throughout California.
It has been said that the Committee on Lodge Support is charged
with the task to eliminate the need for it to exist. With this proud goal
we proceed and hope for increasing Masonic light in every lodge and a
fading need for our committee.

2. Create a lodge vision and a mission for its existence.
3. Avoid failure by developing a written “Lodge Plan” that is
constantly updated.
4. Analyze operations and programming, adapt to improve
projects that also include new ideas, and overcome shortfalls
and situations before they become entrenched problems.
5. Inclusion of – and communication within – a leadership team,
while providing clear, achievable goals that measure success.
The Committee on Lodge Support recognizes that all lodges are
unique in their history and formation. We assist and facilitate lodges
in understanding their unique responsibility to act as stewards of
California Freemasonry, its historical relevance, precepts, landmarks,
and the preservation of Masonic values within their own unique
communities. Lodge individuality strengthens our jurisdiction and
Freemasonry, in general, throughout the world. However, with certainty,
when lodge brethren live by those shared Masonic values of our ritual
and our obligations, harmony prevails and lodges succeed in all their
doings. Our committee therefore encourages lodges to pursue strength
from shared values that are uniquely applied to their lodge.
The Committee on Lodge Support further recognizes that lodge
individuality reflects the public community in which it exists, and more
importantly the collective identity of its membership. Therefore, the
committee encourages all lodges to pursue opportunities to engage
in programs that enrich their communities and neighbors, and that,
consequently, enhance the lives of its brethren. These are the best
practices of strong vibrant lodges.

Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California
This Committee is honored to have had the opportunity to
serve this Grand Lodge in the past Masonic year. Two years ago, the
Committee set certain priorities in furthering its mandate to assist
the hall associations in matters related to management of their real
properties. The two most important of these priorities were:

that the members of this Committee were highly experienced
individuals whose only mission was to help protect the real
property interest of hall associations and their members.

members and to respond to applications in 10 days rather
than 30 days.

70 applications and responded to minimum of three to four weekly
calls from various hall associations. The members of the Committee,
based on their locations, have visited various buildings and rendered
professional advice when such visits were deemed necessary. We are at
a point now where most hall associations call to consult with us before
submitting their applications.
The Grand Lodge has engaged the services of a highly qualified
individual as Director of Real Estate, who works full time for the
Grand Lodge. The hiring of this individual has substantially helped
the Committee and hall associations in performing their respective
responsibilities. We now receive the applications in a much more
organized and complete form and can respond much faster, and
effectively address issues that we find troubling.
The applications that the Committee has reviewed are too
numerous to individually list. However, it is safe to say that we have
dealt with almost all issues that may present themselves in dealing
with real estate. The communication towers that are installed in some
hall association properties have presented the most challenging
issues. Brokers have approached hall associations with promises of
future increases in income in return for long-term, sometimes more

The Committee on Trial Review has carefully examined the
records of all trial matters completed during the past Masonic year. All
Committee votes were unanimous except where otherwise noted.
In each of the matters, unless otherwise noted, the Committee
finds there was compliance with the procedural requirements of the
California Masonic Code.
The following cases were decided by the Trial Masters
after investigation as provided for in California Masonic Code
section 1404.410.
Trial 2689: Masonic charges for perjury were brought
against the Accused. The Accused had executed a
handwritten letter detailing an assault or hazing
he suffered at the hands of Master Masons in the
preparation room prior to his third degree. The letter
and a subsequent investigation resulted in the filing
of Masonic charges against the hazing brothers. At
the hazing brothers’ trial, the Accused claimed he was
forced to make the statements in the letter and, while
under oath, completely retracted that prior statement.
Because the original letter was corroborated, the
hazing brothers were found guilty. The Accused was

Trials 2741 and 2742: On a degree night, the Treasurer of

brothers exited the Lodge room where the argument
escalated to a physical altercation. Brethren, including
the candidate, separated the brothers. Three charges
were filed, the first for use of defamatory, vile, indecent,
profane, abusive or threatening language; the second
for personal violence against a brother; and the third
for acts or actions in material breach of the degrees.
After the event, the two Accused made peace with one
another. They approached the Trial Master seeking to
have the charges dismissed. The Trial Master correctly
refused to dismiss the charges in the belief that the
conduct, especially in front of a candidate, was against
the teachings of Masonry and must be addressed. At the
pretrial conference the parties and their counsel met
and presented a settlement proposal to the Trial Master
which he accepted. Both Accuseds were found guilty
and the penalty set at a reprimand.

Trial 2737 and Trial 2738: These consolidated cases arose
out of the same incident. The Accused were charged
with hazing a candidate while they were serving as
acting stewards by striking him two times prior to the
commencement of his third degree. All pre-trial and
trial proceedings were held jointly with the agreement
of the parties.
Prior to trial the parties stipulated that the candidate,
just after being hoodwinked and prior to his degree
commencing, was indeed assaulted and battered in
the preparation room. As a result, all the elements of
the offenses were established and the only question
remaining for consideration of the Trial Master (trial
by commissioners having been waived) was who
committed the violations of the Code.
The candidate testified at trial that later that evening
the Accused in case number 2737 told him to “take it
like a man, get over it and move on, you can get the next
candidate.” A passing brother heard the comment but
was not sure who said it.
The Trial Master made the following findings: that the
Accused in case number 2737 struck the candidate
causing physical injury and humiliation materially
harming the candidate. He found the Accused in
case number 2738 either also struck the candidate
or observed the first one do it and failed to report it;
moreover, he attempted to cover for the first one. At trial
both stewards denied striking the candidate or seeing
the other do it. Based on the totality of the evidence and
other testimony introduced the Trial Master found both
of their statements to be untruthful.
Based on the foregoing, the Trial Master found the
steward in case number 2737 guilty of physically
striking the candidate and while it was possible the

steward in case number 2738 delivered a blow, it was

The Trial Master concluded this claim was contrary
to the evidence and that the Accused in case number
2738 was untruthful, that there was sufficient evidence
that he caused mental injury and humiliation to the
candidate and materially harmed him, therefore was in
violation of the charged Code sections. The Trial Master
found no mitigating circumstances and set the penalty

Trial 2755: In this matter, the Accused’s professional
license was revoked for violation of the California
Business and Professions Code sections prohibiting
dishonesty, fraud, and embezzlement. The revocation
was in response to charges filed by a client arising out
of the Accused’s handling of the client’s funds. In at
least two instances, the Accused had directly used funds
from the client to pay personal credit card charges.
The licensing board revoked his license in 2005; two
applications for restoration of his license were denied.
His third request for restoration was granted in January
2012, but only under certain restrictions including the
fact that the Accused’s license is a probationary one
through March 2017.

309

Upon review, the Committee determined that the
procedures did not comply with the California Masonic
Code. Moreover, the Committee also found that given
the Trial Master’s finding of unmasonic conduct,
the dismissal of the charges was not supported by
substantial evidence (CMC §1404.910.D.1.)
Being informed of the findings and the potential for
having to re-commence the proceedings, the Accuser
waived any objection to the procedural errors. The
Committee on Trial Review, exercising its authority
found in Code section 1404.910.D. 1 and 2, entered a
finding of guilty.
Having reviewed the matter in full, the Committee
agreed that the acts of the Accused constituted
unmasonic conduct, against the moral law and
constituted acts of moral turpitude. However, due
to mitigating circumstances, including the passage
of time, the payment of substantial restitution,
the restoration of his license by the public agency,
and the acknowledgment by the Accused of his
misconduct, the penalty for the unmasonic conduct
should be fixed at indefinite suspension which will
permit the brothers of the Accused’s Lodge to determine
if he it is appropriate he be restored to membership
in accordance with the procedures outlined in the
California Masonic Code.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for
adoption of the following Resolution:

Case 2580: In 2010, Francisco S. Ibo was expelled by
trial from Masonry for refusal to obey the order of the
Grand Master that he renounce his membership in the
Grand and Glorious Order Knights of the Creeping
Serpent, commonly known as the snakes and that he
provide a list of the members of the organization. In
response to the Grand Master’s order, Mr. Ibo refused to
renounce his membership or provide the list.
Mr. Ibo has now requested restoration of his
membership to this Grand Lodge by submitting a letter
to Grand Master Perry apologizing for his actions and
for the failure to comply with the Grand Maser’s order.
In support of his application he indicating he has been
helping disadvantaged children and would like to be
involved in the charitable aspects of this Grand Lodge.
A request for restoration must address the factors
enunciated in Grand Master Adamson’s Decision No. 3,
that is, whether his current standing, conduct, character
and reputation are such as would make him worthy
of membership in a lodge, the nature of the conduct
which gave rise to his expulsion, the seriousness of the
conduct, the passage of a suitable length of time, the
likelihood he will repeat the conduct, his acceptance
of responsibility, remorse and atonement, his efforts to
make amends for the consequences of his conduct and
recommendations of concerned and knowledgeable
Masons and non-Masons.
His original application failed to address any of the
above factors other than those noted above. In contrast,
the nature of his conduct went well beyond just
refusing to obey a directive of the Grand Master. Mr. Ibo
was an active member of the Snakes, an organization
dedicated to undermining our Grand Lodge and to

have

311

Upon prodding by Grand Lodge, Mr. Ibo supplemented
his application in October of this year and further
stated he had not been involved with the Snakes for
eight years and has no plans to do so in the future and
indicated that he sincerely apologized for the conduct
which led to his expulsion.
Even as supplemented, the application does nothing
to address the other factors enumerated in Decision
No. 3. Mr. Ibo has not submitted any evidence of his
present standing in the community or that his conduct
or character currently are such as would make him
worthy of membership in a lodge. Additionally, he has
submitted no outside verification of his activities in the
last eight years or any information from third parties
corroborating his claims of meritorious conduct. The
Committee also would like to have some assurance that
he will obey directives of the Grand Master if restored
to membership.
Based on the inadequacies in the application, the Committee
recommends a no vote.

Recognized Foreign Grand Lodges 2016
The Grand Lodge of California recognizes all of the Grand Lodges
in the United States published in the 2016 List of Lodges Masonic, which
includes all 50 states and the District of Columbia. In addition, the
Grand Lodge of California recognizes a number of Prince Hall Grand
Lodges and foreign Grand Lodges around the world. The Grand Lodge
of California recognizes some, but not all, of the foreign Grand Lodges
in the 2016 List of Lodges Masonic as well as a number of foreign Grand
Lodges that are not listed therein.
For clarity, the foreign Grand Lodges that are recognized by the
Grand Lodge of California are listed below alphabetically by country.
For those that are published in the 2016 List of Lodges Masonic, the
corresponding page number is provided in parenthesis. Recognized
Grand Lodges that are not published in the 2016 List of Lodges Masonic
are marked with an asterisk (*). The Grand Secretary of the Grand
Lodge of California is responsible for all correspondence with these
Grand Lodges and the lodges under their jurisdiction. Please contact
this office for assistance.
